q: We are affectionate in public but cold behind closed doors. Why?

blocks.x: Before anything begins in a dungeon, two people agree. That is where I learned about structure. What is on. What is off. What is a hard no. How long it will last.

Your living room has none of that. There is no start and no end, and no easy way to say "not tonight" without it turning into a conversation about the state of the relationship. Any reach could be nothing, or it could be everything, so your body gets ready for everything.
Why am I affectionate in public but cold at home?
Because in public the setting gives your touch edges, and at home nothing does.

At a dinner party, a hand on your knee has an end built in. Everyone is still at the table, the pudding arrives, the evening finishes. There is no way for it to go further there, so your body can enjoy it. At home, the same hand has no end built in, and your body has learned that touch there tends to come with a "what's next".
Does it mean the affection in public is fake?
No. The affection is real, and so is the closed door, and both can live in you at the same time.

Loving your partner and a body that stays shut can sit in the same person on the same day. I say that to couples often because it takes so much shame out of the room. What looks like coldness from the outside is usually a brace on the inside, the half second where your body tightens before you have decided anything. In public your body never gets that half second, because the setting has already answered the question.
How do I bring the feeling of public touch home?
Give the touch the same edges the setting gives it in public: a start, an end, and a no that will be heard.
Start on your own. Touch Base: thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say "I am safe right now", and hold for two minutes.
Ask out loud and agree the time. "Can I trace your face for two minutes?" is the kind of question I teach. The answer and the length are said before anything begins.
Say where it is going. Tell each other: this is not going anywhere. Then notice what happens in your body when you know that.
Agree the no. I use a stoplight with my clients. Red stops everything. Orange means slow down and take a breath. Green means keep going. The no gets heard the first time.
Once your body knows how long something lasts and that it can stop, it can show you what it wants. That is the same reason a hand at a party feels easy.
How long should the first agreed touch last?
Two minutes is enough to begin. The aim is a touch with no destination, so your body can learn that it ends where you said it would.

When you are ready for longer, I suggest a date morning over a date night. Plan between 45 and 90 minutes, because by the end of the evening you are tired. One of you sets up the room and tidies it, you put the music on, and you both start clean.

I teach this structure in episode 39 of The Scrumptious Woman, and I walk through Touch Base and the three stages couples move through in episode 36. If every touch at home feels like the opening move of something bigger, why touch always leads to sex goes further into it, and sleeping in the same bed and never touching covers the other end of the same pattern.

To give the question a home, I made the intimacy and communication cards, over 150 cards in the app, for the asking you do before touch. If you would like me beside you for the structure itself, that is what I do at Feel Fully You, and The Beginning is the deepest way in for couples.
Your body braced for good reasons. Patterns can change.

q: Boundary Setting in Intimacy: How Do I Set Boundaries Without Pushing My Partner Away?

blocks.x: Boundary setting in intimacy starts long before the bedroom. Think back to being three or four. An uncle or an auntie comes into the house, and your parents want you to go and give a hug. Everything in your body is retracting. You give the hug anyway, because that is what is expected.
Your body had a no, and it learned that the no could be overridden. It may not even have been you who overrode it. So the question I put to you is how often you override your nos now.
What does boundary setting in intimacy sound like?
It sounds like a no to this one thing, with a when attached.

Each of those starts with a check-in with yourself. What feels aligned and juicy at this moment? What do you have the bandwidth and capacity for? So often we override our capacity and go ahead, because it is easier than a whole discussion.

Do you have to explain? I ask, does it really matter? Do you have to give the explanation, or can you be with your now? It is a simple exercise, and not an easy one. I walk through it in the Scrumptious Woman episode on the power of saying no.
Why do I say yes when my body says no?
A body taught young that its no can be overridden keeps overriding it.

Look back at this week. Where did you say yes to a cup of tea when you really wanted a cappuccino? Where did your partner come in for a kiss, it did not feel nice, and you went ahead? Where did a hand graze your leg on the tube while you froze and said nothing?

There are so many micro moments where we have felt the no and not acknowledged it. Afterwards comes the shame spiral: why did I say yes? I see this in parents, in my couples, and where trauma happened too soon, too fast, too quick. Oftentimes it is sexual, because that is what people come to me for.
How do I learn to feel my no before I need it?
Practise it in daylight, in your body, before it has to be said under pressure.
Anchor yourself first. Touch Base®: thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say “I am safe right now”, and hold for two minutes.
Notice the moments. Find the ones this week where your body braced and you went ahead anyway.

Practise a no with your clothes on. You cannot trust a body whose no has never been respected, so practise a no in daylight until it is boring, and until you recognise what your no, your yes and your curiosity feel like.

I teach that last step with offers and requests, written up in how to enjoy touch again when it started to feel like a chore. If you want a week of it, The Sacred No is a seven-day, body-based experience in the app for feeling your yes and your no one day at a time.
What if I have never felt safe saying no?
Then the no is the work, and it starts with a body that has an experience of its own yes and no.

In the room, I teach a body that has learned the world is not safe that this touch is different. Your no holds, and your yes is required. I work as an intimacy and touch coach in the UK, and this is the centre of what I do.
A year from now, are you still saying yes to the cup of tea while your body wants a cappuccino?

q: Can intimacy cards actually help a dead bedroom or sexless marriage?

blocks.x: You have probably typed this question late at night, and most of what came back was either a miracle promise or someone telling you it is hopeless.
Here is what I have actually watched, across more than 650 couples.

A bedroom does not go dead because the love left. It goes quiet in stages. First the conversations thin out. Then every touch starts carrying a question inside it. Then one of you starts going to bed early, pretending to be asleep, hoping the other will not try. By the time the bedroom is silent, the talking has usually been silent for years.
That order matters, because it is also the way back in.
What the cards actually do

The Intimacy and Communication Cards will not manufacture desire. Nothing external can. Desire returns to a body that trusts the conditions around it, and trust is rebuilt in conversation before it is rebuilt in touch.

What the cards do is make that conversation possible without either of you having to improvise it. One card, read aloud. Three answers each, going deeper with each round. Switch. Fifteen minutes. The structure means nobody has to find an opening line, nobody has to steer, and nobody gets ambushed. A guarded body relaxes inside structure in a way it never does inside “we need to talk”.

The love had been in the room the entire time. The container was what had been missing.

q: Can the spark come back in a long-term relationship?

blocks.x: The first months were electric. Now it is quieter, and one or both of you has started wondering if the love has gone with it.
What dropped was intensity. Intensity was never the love.

The early charge is a neurochemical storm: dopamine, norepinephrine, a racing heart, no appetite. It is the body's way of bonding before the slower chemistry of attachment takes over. It always calms. For bodies trained on intensity, the calm feels like death, and the mind writes a story: we have lost something. The affairs start here. The restless scanning. What is being chased is the activation of your own system. The new person is just the trigger.
What is actually available

Warmth instead of fire. Safety instead of urgency. A hand on your back you lean into without thinking. For many couples this is the first time their bodies have ever experienced closeness without threat, and at first it can feel like nothing, because the body is scanning for the old signal.
How it gets built

Deliberately. In my twelve-week programme for couples, The Beginning, touch dates start at three minutes. One leads, one receives, no switching. Capacity builds week by week, and by week twelve something has shifted that neither partner can quite explain. She has stopped scanning his face. He has stopped wondering if he is doing it right.
The couple who had not touched in 23 years went on a second honeymoon after three months of this. The love had been in the room the entire time.
I have watched more than 650 couples cross this exact bridge. The quiet is not the end. It is the doorway.

q: What Are Good Communication Exercises for Couples to Feel Closer?

blocks.x: A boy I mentored at a boarding school found me on Instagram a few years after we worked together. He had finished university and started his first job. His message said the session where I showed him what it means when I glance at the clock, start putting my files away and fold my arms had stayed with him. He can now read when someone is ready to close a conversation.

At the time he looked at me blankly. “I’ve seen you do that every time at the end of a lesson,” he said. I had to spell out what my body was saying, because nobody had ever done it for him. Couples sit in the same blank. Words cross the room, the meaning does not arrive, and neither of you has been shown how to check.
What makes a communication exercise work for couples?

It pulls speaking and receiving apart, so one of you says something and the other takes it in before anyone replies. Most of us listen in order to jump in with our own thing. That is how you can say something clearly and still not feel heard, even though your partner caught every word.

This is one of the biggest eye-openers for the couples I work with. After years together the complaint is almost always the same: my partner never listens. The aim of a good exercise is that you are understood. Your partner does not have to agree. Your partner says thank you once the message has landed.
Two habits shut the other person down completely, so I ask couples to drop them:
Comparisons, as in “why can’t you be more like…”
“You never…”
How do you set up a communication exercise with your partner?
You plan it in, the way you would plan a date. Ambushing your partner in the kitchen with “we need to talk” puts both nervous systems on guard before a word is said. Here is the setup I teach:
Ask first: “Do you have fifteen minutes?” Pick a time that suits you both.
Put phones on silent or airplane mode and out of reach.
Make sure the children are elsewhere.
Agree that you both need to win.
Keep it to communicating. Nothing gets solved in this window.
I walk through the whole exercise in episode 2 of my podcast. The structure behind it is also laid out in why every conversation ends in silence.
What if your body shuts down before you even start?

Start smaller than a conversation. When one of you is already braced, the words “shall we talk?” will brace you both. I teach that the first step is one small act in the body, with a clear start and a clear end.
That small act is Touch Base®. Press your thumb to your forefinger and feel the ridges. Tell yourself, “I am safe right now.” Hold for two minutes.

Your mind may shout at you to go faster. That is information, so let it shout. If locking yourself in the loo is the only place you get two minutes, that counts. I explain why the body freezes before it acts in this episode. Structured prompts, structured communication and structured touch all lean on that sense of safety, and it is where the closeness starts to feel possible.
Which communication skills for couples exercises help the most?

The ones that train three skills: listening to understand, saying thank you when you have understood, and leaving comparisons out of the room. Whether an exercise comes from a couples therapy workbook or from a deck of cards, that is the test I would put it through.

What works for one person does not necessarily work for another, so keep what lands and drop what does not. Couples who want the structure on the table, ready to use, often start with the Intimacy and Communication Cards.
Can communication exercises help a couple close to divorce?

They have for couples I have worked with. On the podcast I said this method helped three couples from the brink of divorce become intimate again, and two of them went on a honeymoon and renewed their vows.
The couples came to me tired of the same row. What changed was being heard without having to win, and that was enough to make touch feel possible again.
If you want to see where the two of you are stuck, the work at Feel Fully You starts there.
You do not have to find better words. You need fifteen minutes, a phone in another room, and someone who says thank you.

q: We tried couples therapy and it didn't work. What do we do now?

blocks.x: For years I asked my husband to see a marriage counsellor with me. He did not think it was necessary. When we finally went, the therapist said something that I have thought about every year since, working with couples. He told her husband that she had climbed the mountain, was already on her way down, and he was still running behind her trying to catch up.
That line holds most of what I see in the couples who write to me after therapy has not fixed their sex life. The sessions probably gave them real language. The pattern sits at a different altitude.
Why didn't couples therapy fix our sex life?

Because talking works on the slowest system in the room, and the loop that ends touch in a long marriage runs on the fastest. She goes still. He reads the stillness as rejection and stops reaching. She reads the stopping as proof she was right to go still. Nobody names it, and a few years on neither of them is reaching at all.

An argument has never once ended a marriage. The accumulation does, a thousand small reaches that landed wrong, until she has grieved the marriage privately long before she says a word out loud. By the time he can speak about it, their bodies have already voted.
Is it normal to know exactly what's wrong and still not change it?

Yes, and in my work it is the most common thing I hear. I recorded a whole episode on it, because my DMs are full of it: I know what is wrong, I know what would help, so why can't I make myself do it?

Knowing was never what was in the way. The moment you act, you admit this is not fine as it is, and that one sentence threatens the house, the routine, the holidays, the story you have told others. So the nervous system does the most protective thing it knows. It freezes. That is why I never start with a big conversation. A braced body cannot take one in. We start with one small act, with structure, time and touch.
What should we try after couples therapy for intimacy?
Try body-based work in this order, because each step makes the next one possible:
Separate work first. Two activated systems cannot do this work in the same room at the start, so each of you builds capacity individually.
Structured touch dates. Short and time-limited at first, growing as safety does.
A protected date morning. Once a week, just the two of you, no phones, nothing allowed to interrupt you tuning towards each other on purpose.

I have watched this order work. A couple who had lived as roommates for 23 years were, three months in with exactly this structure, on a second honeymoon and having sex. I am not shocked by it any more. I have lived it, and I have seen it.
If you want that with me in the room, the couples VIP day is where it starts, and I tell the whole of my own marriage story in episode 33 of the podcast.
What changes once the body is part of it?

The couple stop circling the same evening. In another couple's case we took sex off the table first, which was easy because it had not happened in so many years. Three months later they were on a second honeymoon, and it was their best year in business too. What happens in a couple's touch life bleeds into everything.

If you are not sure whether it is time for more help, this page on when to get help with intimacy is a good next read, and you can see how I work on the home page of Feel Fully You, where I am an intimacy and touch coach in the UK for couples who love each other and cannot find the door back in.
Talk therapy meets the words. This work meets the body, where the pattern actually lives.

q: Is it normal to crave touch from other people in a long-distance relationship?

blocks.x: You love him. You've told your friends that a dozen times this month, and meant it every time. You've also caught yourself lingering a beat too long on a hug from someone else, noticing a hand on your back at a party, feeling something you didn't expect to feel, and then spending the drive home wondering what that means about you.

It means your skin has a need a video call cannot meet. Touch is not a bonus feature of a relationship. It sits on the same shelf as sleep and food, and a body that goes weeks or months without it will register the deficit whether or not you gave it permission to. Feeling something when a stranger's hand lands on your shoulder is not your body choosing someone else. It's your body registering contact, because contact is what it has been missing.
Why this isn't a loyalty pattern

A craving is not a decision, and it is not the same thing as wanting to act on it. The two get confused constantly, mostly because we've been taught that any physical response to someone who isn't our partner must mean the relationship is failing. It usually means something simpler: distance has a cost, and the body pays it first.
What to actually do with it

Naming it honestly is the first move, to yourself and, when you're ready, to him. The second is building deliberate touch back into the contact you do have: the video call where you're both doing the same physical gesture at the same time, the letter that arrives with something to hold, the visit planned with actual touch time built into it rather than left to chance. And your own body still needs tending in the meantime. Two minutes of your own hand, thumb to forefinger, slow, saying I am safe right now, is not a replacement for him. It is maintenance on a system that still needs some contact to run.
The need is real. Meeting it honestly, in the relationship you're actually in, is different work from pretending it isn't there.

q: Dissociation during sex: why you leave your body, and how to stay present

blocks.x: You dissociate during sex because your body learned that leaving is safer than feeling, and it tends to do it right when the touch gets most intense. Juliette Karaman, an intimacy and touch expert in the UK, works with this as a protection your body can retrain, one slow minute at a time.
You are lying there, and somewhere along the way you have gone up to the ceiling. You can see it happening. You just are not in it. Then it is over, and you wonder where you went.
Why do I dissociate during sex?
Something in the moment arrived too soon or too fast for your body to take in, so your attention stepped out to keep you safe.

Trauma is anything that happened too soon or too fast for your body or your psyche to take in. Big events count, and so do small ones. Your body files every single one. Then, right at the peak of intimacy, it answers before you do.

One of the three Touch Patterns I work with is the Wanderer: “My attention can leave the experience.” At the very moment that could crack you open, you leave, and watch it happen from somewhere up there. What brings you back, in my experience, is capacity, built slowly.
What does zoning out during sex look like?
It often looks like being in the room and somewhere else at the same time. Zoning out during sex can show up as any of these.
You watch it happen from somewhere up there.
You look up at the ceiling and mentally run the clock.
You check his face and wonder how long this is going to take.
You go numb, or feel far less than you want to.
Every one of these is protection. Your body is doing the job it learned, and it can learn a new one. Here is what each sign tends to mean, and what I teach for it.

Sometimes it is. It was for me. My subconscious buried my date rape for over twenty-five years, and I would have said I was fine. It came back in a BDSM class, of all places, when my body started shaking. My body had been carrying it the whole time.

Start with safety, add a structure your body can trust, and build capacity slowly, with your yes required at every step.

Come back without shame. If your attention leaves, nothing is taken from you while you are gone. Come back with the forearm practice below, warmth, weight and where.

Then the weight, when you stop hovering and let it land. Then where: can you feel the edge of it? That is a touch no one is taking from you. You gave it to yourself, on your own terms.

Why winging it fails

One of you is defending: how do I not come out of this the villain. Both of you are fixing: how do we end this conversation quickly and intact.
Three jobs, zero listening. That is why the same conversation has circled for years without landing.

Three answers each, going deeper each round, so the first answer, the rehearsed one, is never the last. The listener receives with thank you, clarify that, summarise that, and does nothing else. The structure is doing the safety work that willpower has been failing to do for years.

EMDR reaches a specific moment and processes the charge it holds. It gave me access to the moments that carry the most charge, through bilateral stimulation, eye movements and cross-body work.
The memory stays. What changes is that one moment stops commanding the whole system.

The moment I reach for is often the first time someone learned that reaching out meant getting hurt. The childhood bedroom. The dinner table that went quiet before it got loud. EMDR processes the charge in that memory so the body stops sending its alarm based on outdated information.
Each tool I use reaches something the others cannot.

q: How do I overcome fear of intimacy and feel safe opening up?

blocks.x: When women ask me how to overcome fear of intimacy, I think of a courtyard in the mountains of Lebanon. At a retreat I ran there, I paired the women up for a simple exercise: notice what they see in each other. Value neutral, no judgement.

Afterwards I asked how many had been judging themselves. Hands shot up, and the courtyard filled with giggles. Then I asked whether they had judged their partner. Most said not really. They had been so afraid of doing it wrong that they had barely seen the other person at all.
Fear of intimacy often looks like constant monitoring while someone stands right beside them. It is a body doing its job, and it can be taught a different job.
Why am I afraid of opening up to someone I love?

Because your body learned at some point that being open was not always safe, and it protects you faster than you can think. You can love someone and your body can still stay shut. Those two live together.

I call the first part of it the brace. A hand lands on your back, and before you have decided anything, your body tightens. You override it and let the hand stay. The brace has already happened underneath the thought, and it often goes back to something much earlier than the person standing next to you.
Can I overcome fear of intimacy by just trying harder?

No. A nervous system organised around threat does not open on demand. It opens when the conditions are consistent enough, and trustworthy enough, that the body begins to believe it will not be punished for opening.

At that retreat, the structure of the day was the safety. I told the women exactly what would happen and when they would get their phones back, and every session built on the last. When the brain can anticipate what comes next, the vigilance load drops.
More effort, more candles, more things that bring in sensation can add input to a body that is already guarded. Predictability is what helps first.
How can I overcome my fear of intimacy and feel safe opening up?
Make safety the first step, then open up in layers. In order:

Begin with an anchor that is entirely yours. Touch Base: thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say "I am safe right now", and hold for two minutes. Do it somewhere you really are safe, such as your bed or your car.
Ask yourself one question. What do I need right now to feel even more safe? Start with yourself before anyone else is involved.
Choose the container before the conversation. Know when it starts, when it ends and what will happen in between, so your body can anticipate it.
Let the first answer be the safe one. The first few times you answer a deep question, you surface swim. Each repetition goes a little deeper. The question stays the same and your willingness grows.
The Intimacy and Communication Cards were built for step four. One question, asked and answered in layers, with a start and an end.
What happens when it starts to feel safe?

The women found out what they had been holding. After they wrote what they desired on post-it notes and put them on the wall, several of them phoned home. One told her husband she had been assuming for years that she knew what he wanted, and had left no room for him to surprise her. She had not known that until she saw her own desire on the wall.

That is what opening up looks like once it is safe: curiosity coming back before closeness does. I tell the story in full in my essay Creating Safety, and I talk about the brace and Touch Base in the Season 2 episode on why a date night changed nothing, on the podcast.

If something in your body shuts down as someone gets closer, my answer on why the body shuts down when things get close goes further. Or start with the Touch Reset Quiz.
A body that has been shown it is safe has somewhere to open to.

q: Why do I go through the motions during intimacy and check out halfway through?

blocks.x: You are there and you are not there. Your hands know the choreography. Your mind is on the ceiling, the calendar, the sound of the boiler. It fades halfway through. Afterwards you feel further away than before you started.
This is not a desire failure. It is your body managing a situation it never fully agreed to.

Within a minute of him reaching for you, you are expected somewhere your body has not arrived at yet. It is still at the sink, still running the day. It never got the chance to catch up. So it does the only thing it can do: it performs the motions, feels the disconnection, and files it away.
Why trying harder makes it worse

Every attempt to force presence teaches your body that its absence will be overridden too. The body does not open on command. It opens inside a container it trusts: clear walls, a way in, a way back. A guarded body will not let go in open space.
Small enough to stay for

In my work, touch starts at three minutes. One person gives. One receives. No switching, no expectation, nothing that escalates without agreement. People think I am joking. Three minutes is where capacity lives. A body that has performed for years cannot sustain thirty minutes of genuine presence, and three minutes of real contact is more than most couples have had in years.

The couple who had not touched in 23 years started exactly there. Three months later they took a second honeymoon. The love had been in the room the entire time. The container was what had been missing.
More than 980 women have sat across from me with this exact pattern. It is the one I know best.

q: How can an intimacy coach help rebuild emotional connection in a relationship?

blocks.x: The morning I decided to leave my marriage, my body went light. I had been carrying something on my shoulders for so long that I had stopped feeling it, and in one night it was gone. My chest could take a full exhale.
Karim and I divorced over a decade ago. We are still completely a family. Friends at parties ask how we managed it, and the honest answer is that it can be taught.

The most useful thing I ever heard about emotional connection came from the counsellor we saw together, years after I first asked. He told my husband I had already climbed the mountain and was on my way down, while he was still running up behind me, trying to catch up.
I have thought about that line in almost every room I have been in with couples since. I told the whole story on the podcast, in the episode about the moment my body knew my marriage was over.
What does an intimacy coach actually do for couples?

An intimacy coach finds the small moment where connection keeps breaking, and gives two people a structure to meet each other there again. In all my years working with couples, what wears a marriage down is the accumulation: the reach that lands wrong, again and again. One argument almost never does it on its own.

Here is the shape I watch most. She goes still when a reach lands wrong. He reads the stillness as rejection and stops reaching. She reads the stopping as proof she was right to go still. Soon neither of them reaches at all, nobody has named it, and one day she is standing in the kitchen with a stranger who shares her mortgage. It runs the other way round just as often.

By the time he notices something is wrong, she has usually grieved the relationship privately, long before she says a word out loud. There is a whole page on why she goes quiet, and what that silence is protecting.
People call this intimacy coaching, intimate coaching or relationship intimacy coaching. With me it means the same practical work:
Find the reach that lands wrong, so both of you can see it happening instead of living inside it.
Take sex off the table at the start, so the pressure leaves the room.
Learn to talk again, then work out what each of you actually likes, so you can ask for it.
Bring touch back with no destination, week after week, until each body trusts it.
What does intimacy coaching for couples look like week to week?

It looks like three small, protected habits that rebuild what years of missed reaches wore down. Everything on this list is practice I have lived, which is how I know it rebuilds a nervous system and a relationship.

A date morning, once a week. Protected time, just the two of you, no phones, nothing allowed to interrupt you tuning towards each other on purpose. Mornings, because by the end of the night you are both tired.
Fifteen minutes of structured communication. One card from the Communication & Intimacy Cards, held inside the Dyad I teach, so one honest thing gets said and heard every week.

Touch with no destination. Non-sexual, offered with curiosity, week after week. Very few teach this piece, because the assumption is that touch is either nothing or sex. A whole nervous system lives between those two, holding years of what it learned about safety.
Everything I teach at Feel Fully You starts with the body feeling safe first. Words land differently once it does.

No, and I would be wary of any coach who promised to. I am not here to save your relationship. I am best friends with my ex-husband, and I have helped tens of couples uncouple and divorce beautifully, because sometimes that is what the relationship actually needs.
Some of you will leave. Some of you will stay and it will be unrecognisable. Both are a good outcome.

q: How do I tell my partner I need more intimacy without hurting them or starting a fight?

blocks.x: You have rehearsed this conversation in the shower for months. Every version ends badly in your head, so you keep not having it, and the distance keeps growing anyway.

The conversation goes wrong for one reason: it arrives as a verdict. “We never touch anymore” is a grade, and a failing one. The body on the receiving end hears the failure before it hears the longing, braces, and defends. Now you are having a fight about the conversation instead of the closeness.
The three rules

Want, never lack. “I miss you. I want more of us” contains the same information as “we never touch anymore”, and lands completely differently. One is an invitation toward you. The other is evidence against them.

Neutral ground, never the bedroom. Walking, driving, washing up. Daylight. Never right after a refusal, never at midnight, never mid-argument. The bedroom is the most charged room in the house; the conversation about it should happen furthest from it.
Side by side beats face to face. Eye contact reads as intensity to a braced body. Walking or driving lets the words land without the spotlight.
Then give it a structure

One conversation will not carry years of distance, and it should not have to. What works is small and repeated: one question at a time, three answers each, and the listener only receives. Thank you. Clarify that. Summarise that. No defending, no fixing.

This is exactly what the Intimacy and Communication Cards hold for you. The card asks, so neither of you has to. Fifteen minutes, once or twice a week. I have watched hundreds of couples have the conversation they postponed for a decade this way, and the most common thing they say afterwards is: that was so much easier than the version in my head.
The version in your head is a fight. The version with structure is fifteen minutes. I have watched the second one work, couple after couple.

q: How Do I Ask for the Kind of Touch I Actually Want?

blocks.x: A woman in my room told her husband exactly what she wanted. She wanted to be fed a strawberry from his mouth.
He pulled a face. “Oh no, that’s disgusting.” A hard no, in front of me.
She giggled, and I watched what the giggle was doing. Her body was working out the sum: I asked for what I want, and I can’t have it.
So I slowed everything down. I asked her permission. I read her body. Often that is what is missing: the asking for permission, and the slowness.
Why is it so hard to ask for the touch I want?
It is hard because most of us have learned that what we want is too much, so we stop asking and take what arrives.

I hear that expectation in couples all the time: I am demanding too much. The cost is quiet. The touch you want never comes, and you live on scraps. I start couples with asking for small things outside the bedroom, because once that works, the same asking can move into touch.
I talk about this in episode 34 of The Scrumptious Woman, and it connects to why you can feel it with someone else and not the man you love.
What do I actually say while the touch is happening?
Adjust the touch in the moment, in plain words, and keep adjusting until it is just right.
“A bit slower.”
“A bit to the left.”
“A bit to the right.”

Say yes out loud when something lands. I call it the yes stroke. When I work with a couple who want more intense touch, I ask for a check-in on every touch: can you feel that? Every time it is a yes, say yes. That trains the body’s capacity, your partner gets real answers, and you hear your own yes out loud.

It may be a hell of awkward at first, and that is where the beauty is. If you can stay with the awkwardness over one small request, you can stay with it when the touch is somewhere that matters. It is all building capacity.
How do I say maybe or stop without a long conversation?
Use one word, a colour. I teach a stoplight, and whatever colour you are is only information.

The stoplight is part of my Touch Map, where you rate one touch at a time and learn to steer it until it lands. Before any of it, I teach Touch Base® on your own: thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say “I am safe right now”, and hold for two minutes.
What if my partner gets defensive or says no?
Ask about the touch itself, because for a lot of men feedback lands as a verdict.

In the couples I work with, being told that something has not been provided lands in him as a verdict on whether he is a good man. What his body receives, before your sentence has even finished, is you have failed. He is defending the feeling of having failed you, and he is doing it without meaning to.

That is why I teach adjusting the touch, with no review of the man attached. When it goes wrong, and it will, you can pause and say, “let’s do that over again.” I come back to this in episode 40 of The Scrumptious Woman. When the answer is no, slow down and ask permission again, the way I did in that room.

A year from now, are you still lying there hoping it lands, or are you saying “a bit to the left”?

q: How do I feel safe being touched again after trauma?

blocks.x: I am mid-recording for episode 7 of my podcast when a wasp turns up in the room. I'm allergic. I don't panic about wasps any more, and still I get up, try to close the window, hunt for it, telling myself it's fine.

Afterwards I notice what I skipped: a tightening in my chest, in my hips, in my sacrum. A slight freeze, so subtle I never felt it arrive. What brought me back was my out-breath. I breathed out for longer than I breathed in, and my body came back on board.
If a wasp can do that to me, a hand can do it to you. That is where being touched again after trauma starts: with a body that needs to hear, in its own language, that it is safe.
How do I feel safe being touched again after trauma?

You feel safe by letting your body lead and giving it small amounts of touch it can say yes to, starting with touch you give yourself. Safety is something a body has to feel. Understanding it in your head is a different job.

Talking about what happened is the top-down route. It builds awareness and helps you spot your patterns, and it often leaves out the feedback loop from the body. The bottom-up route begins in the body, which is why I work with somatic touch alongside talking.
Why does my body feel unsafe when my mind knows I am safe?

Because the part of you that decides what is safe runs below thought, and it has not had the news yet. On episode 7 I say it straight to the listener: you have already survived it, and your body does not always know.
That gap is why reassurance from a loving partner can land as nothing. Your body is waiting for evidence it can feel.
What do I do first, before anyone touches me?
Start with your breath and one anchor, alone. Here is the order I use:
Pause. Notice where your breath goes: upper chest, or lower, into your belly.
Breathe out for longer than you breathe in. This is the move that brought me back from the wasp.
Touch Base®. Thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say “I am safe right now”, and hold for two minutes.
Go slower than seems necessary. I have watched people go deep into breathwork before they are quite ready for it, when their nervous system is not yet regulated.

Seven days of guided self-touch with my voice in your ear, so your body leads and you decide how far each day goes.
Who or what else can help my body feel safe?

A calm, grounded presence helps, because nervous systems co-regulate. I have a whippet who is massively grounded most of the time, and being near her grounds me. Older dogs tend to do this best; a puppy is too hyper.

Then your body has been given room, and you do not have to work through what surfaces by yourself.

q: How to get turned on when you feel disconnected from your body

blocks.x: How to get turned on is a question about your own body first, before anyone else enters the room. Juliette Karaman, an intimacy and touch expert in the UK, teaches exactly this: safety first, then slow, specific touch, until your skin starts answering again.
That is me. A woman sits across from me and tells me she wants to want her partner again. Her whole plan has been waiting for him to flip the switch back on. He can’t. It was never his job.
What does getting turned on mean?
Getting turned on means your body is alive, full stop, before any other human comes close to it. I call it scrumptiousness.

It is the life force running through you. The thing that has you move your shoulders a certain way. Maybe a little lust-filled, maybe a bit taboo. It wants to meet the world and meet another body. It starts with you, always alone.
Why can’t I get turned on when I feel disconnected from my body?
Your nervous system decides whether it is safe to open before your mind gets a say. You cannot think your way into aliveness.

Stephen Porges spent his career on this and called it neuroception. Your body has to register safety first. Only then does it let itself swell and open. So when low libido and that cut-off feeling arrive together, the question I ask is this: when did you stop feeling safe enough in your own body to turn yourself on at all?
Numb counts too. Numb is also a sensation, a lack of sensation, and it tells you where to start.
How do I turn myself on, on my own?
Start with safety, then give yourself three minutes of slow touch and ask one question: is that a yes? This is how to turn yourself on without any pressure to perform.
Touch Base®. Thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say “I am safe right now”, and hold for two minutes.
Find the inside of your wrist. Turn one hand palm up. Find the soft patch between the heel of your hand and the start of your forearm.
Stroke it slowly. Two fingers of your other hand. Can you feel it? Is your body saying yes to that?
Change one thing at a time. The other direction. Lighter, almost grazing. Your nails instead of your finger pads. Watch your hand, then close your eyes.
Notice which one your skin answers to. That is where your own map of touch begins.

Most women have no idea at first. That is the honest answer, and it is the right one. Four women came up to me recently and said they could not feel anything on the inside of their wrist, and thought they must be frigid. The difficulty means the exercise is working.
What are ways to get aroused if I feel stressed or numb?
Make it smaller, slower and safer than you think it needs to be. For a stressed or numb body, how to get aroused is mostly about the conditions you set.
Touch Base every day. Every day, so safety becomes something your body expects.
Your little bundles of joy. A bath. Oils on your skin. You might call this self-care. I call these my little bundles of joy.
Self Touch Dates. Specific and small enough that you can build on each one.
Let numb be there. Notice it, stay with it, and keep the touch slow enough that you can feel every single stroke.
Your skin is the biggest organ you have, and it craves touch. Often the very touch you have not yet given yourself.
Why can I get turned on alone but not with my partner?
Some of what you learn alone travels into the bedroom with a partner, and some of it does not. Researchers in Essex measured this, and split body awareness into three separate skills.

So the noticing is worth three minutes of your life, because it travels. The trusting part needs another person in the room. You cannot trust a body whose no has never been respected. Picture it a year from now, exactly as it is. Same ceiling, same clock. Then picture three slow minutes with the inside of your wrist, and your skin saying yes.

q: How do I get her to trust me again?

blocks.x: Most men try to rebuild trust with words. The big conversation. The promise. The explanation of what will be different this time.
Her mind may accept every word. Her body keeps its own books.

Trust rebuilds through evidence, and evidence is physical. It is you staying in the room when she closes. It is you hearing something that stings without making her carry your reaction. It is you noticing one of her brief openings, the breath dropping, the eye contact lengthening by a beat, and meeting it with presence instead of pouncing on it.
The count her body keeps

Every time her signal is seen and nothing bad happens, her body files it. Every time an opening is missed or a disclosure gets punished, it files that too. You cannot argue with the ledger. You can only add to it, one data point at a time, for longer than feels fair.
This is slower than you want. It is also the only thing I have seen work, across more than 650 couples.
What it makes possible

A former army officer came to me after six weeks of this work. On the morning of his in-person day, his partner sent me a message: I could always depend on him. There is now a steadfastness alongside a vulnerability. He leads from feeling, not from training.
That sentence is what her trust returning sounds like. Steadfastness alongside vulnerability. It was built in moments smaller than he thought counted.
The part you are afraid you have already ruined, I have probably already sat with. It moves.

q: We stopped having sex and now even a hug feels loaded. What do we do?

blocks.x: Picture a hand on a shoulder while someone stacks the dishwasher. The shoulder goes still. A joke arrives, or a sudden reminder of something that needs doing. The hand cools in mid-air, and the person it belongs to is left wondering what just happened.
Couples describe this to me all the time. Nobody refused anything and nobody said a word, and yet a hug that used to be nothing at all now has weight on it.
Why does a hug feel loaded when we have stopped having sex?
Because the hug has started to carry a question. Your body reads every reach as the first step toward something it is not sure it can do.

That reading is a reflex, and it is older than the two of you. Somewhere along the line a body learns that a reach means a test is coming, and that closeness arrives with a bill. Distance feels survivable. Closeness feels like exposure. So it steps back, usually in about half a second.
I know this from the inside. My own body kept me slightly braced and slightly gone, even on the days I was fully there. You cannot be fully met by someone while a part of you is guarded.
Does it mean my partner has stopped wanting me?
Almost never. A partner who goes still when you reach is usually bracing, and the heart is still in the room.

When you say "I miss you", a braced nervous system can hear "you are not enough". A bid for closeness and a criticism land in the same place, and for many men that place is the fear of not providing enough. The brace runs in both directions, so if you are the one who stiffens when your partner approaches, the same half second is happening in you.
If you read the distance as proof that your partner has checked out, you start to chase, and chasing lands as one more demand. Neither of you is the villain in this loop.
How do I know if this is the right moment to reach?
Read before you reach. Ten seconds of noticing tells you whether a touch will land, and your partner never needs to know you did it.
Is your partner's body warm and loose, or cool and held?
Is your partner settled, or perched and ready to move?
Is your partner's attention in the room with you, or already somewhere else?

If the answer is cool, perched and gone, leave the reach for later and give something with no ask inside it. Sit near your partner and say nothing. A calm body next to a braced one tends to settle it. Closeness that wants nothing back may be the thing neither of you has had in a long time.
How do we start touching again if even a hug feels loaded?
Start smaller than a conversation. "Shall we talk?" braces both of you, so I begin with one small act and a structure around it.
Start on your own. Touch Base: thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say "I am safe right now", and hold for two minutes.
Ask before any touch. One question, back and forth: "Tell me, are you present enough for me to touch you right now?"
Give the question a home. I use the intimacy and communication cards, over 150 cards in the app, for exactly this kind of back and forth before touch.
Once a body has been shown that it is safe, desire can come back. Most people skip that step and go straight to what they want, and a body that has not been asked has nothing to say yes with.

I talk through the pull-away in episode 37 of The Scrumptious Woman. If the same loop sounds like the bed you share, we sleep in the same bed but never touch has the three stages, and when he does not want to be touched goes further into the other side of the reach.

When your partner is ready to look at the other half of it, send over the Touch Reset Quiz. Working through it with a guide is what I do at Feel Fully You, and The Beginning is the deepest way in for couples.
Your body braced for good reasons. Patterns can change.

q: Why Do I Flinch When My Partner Surprises Me With Affection?

blocks.x: In a lot of my videos you will hear me say two words to Alex, my fiancé. "You may."
I am not being coy. I am giving him permission out loud, so my body learns that a hand arriving is followed by something good. It took years, and it was necessary.
Why do I flinch when my partner surprises me with affection?
Because a surprise leaves your body no time to agree. The hand arrives first, your yes arrives second, and the flinch happens in between.

Your partner can do everything right and your body still responds the way it has learned to. That tightening is the half second I call the brace. It happens before you decide anything, so it does not check who is touching you or how kind the hand is.
Does the flinch mean I don't want my partner?
Very often it does not. Couples describe a kind hand, a person they love, and a body that braced anyway.

Notice which touches your body receives well, the ones you saw coming or the ones that appeared from behind. That tells you what your body is asking for. If the flinch comes with a locked body or a far away feeling, I wrote about the freeze response as well.
What changes when my partner asks first?
Asking first gives your body a yes it can see coming. In my words: "May I?" "Yes." The touch happens on my word, in my time. That is where both the safety and the charge come from.

Alex and I talked about this one weekend after drawing three of my cards. The first one read: tell me, when it comes to sex, what is a hard no? We gave exactly the same answer. It opened up a beautiful way of connecting, and I talk about it on episode 35 of The Scrumptious Woman.
The intimacy and communication cards give a couple a place to ask before touch, with over 150 cards in the app.
How long does it take for the flinch to settle?
It may take years, and it is necessary. Mine did, and I will not promise you quick.
What shortens the road is small touches that repeat, each one followed by something good. Each one takes seconds. 31 Touch Points is the two of you, three minutes a day, £27.
What can I do on my own while my body learns?
Start with an anchor that belongs to you, and give your yes out loud.
Touch Base. Thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say "I am safe right now", and hold for two minutes.
Say your yes out loud. When you choose a touch, say so, the way I say "You may". It tells your body that the touch is happening on your word.

His mind is not the one in charge at that moment. I tell this story on episode 10 of my podcast, because the machinery that shut him down on a plane is the same machinery that shuts you down when someone you love moves close.
Why does my body shut down when someone gets close?

Your body shuts down because closeness has been filed under danger somewhere below your awareness, and the shutdown is the protection. The active, thinking part of your brain goes offline and you are left in a response, with no choice about it.
In that dorsal shutdown, the cognitive part of the brain goes offline. Closeness has not hurt you in this moment. Your body is reacting to what closeness once meant.
Why can't I think my way out of it?

Because more than 80% of everyday actions are run by the subconscious, and the shutdown lives there. I say this on the episode: we do not know how we breathe, and we do not consciously direct it. The subconscious drives that pattern, and it also drives the pattern of shutting down.
Facts reach only the part of you that is online, and in a shutdown that part is offline. That is why insight alone can leave you understanding your shutdown in detail while it keeps happening.
Is shutting down the same as freezing or dissociating?
They are cousins, and what you notice in the moment tells you which one you are in:
What helps a body that shuts down?

What helps is moving through the shutdown rather than around it, and giving your subconscious a new way to keep you safe. My own position, which I come back to on the podcast, is that the only way out is through, feeling every sensation, emotion and everything that comes up.
Catch the first sign. A held breath, a tight jaw, a stillness in the hips. These come earlier than the blankness.
Come back with Touch Base®. Thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say “I am safe right now”, and hold for two minutes.

Go through the pattern in pieces. In RRRR, Rapid Release Rewire Restore, we move through the images, the thoughts and the body sensations of the shutdown until the old belief that you are unsafe loosens.
Let the subconscious find another way. Hypnotherapy asks it, directly, to find a different way of keeping you safe, because its job is to keep you safe.
When this works, the biggest change is choice. For you, choice means staying or stepping away as your own decision.
Seven days of guided self-touch with my voice in your ear, a gentle place to start feeling again.
When should I get help with it?

Get help when the shutdown keeps costing you closeness, or when you notice you have been managing around it for years. As an intimacy and touch coach in the UK, I work one to one in a VIP day, and I match the tool to the person, from EMDR and hypnotherapy to Somatic Experiencing. If feeling safe in touch is what you are after, read how to feel safe being touched after trauma next.
A shutdown is your body keeping you safe. Choice is what it can learn to give back.

q: Why am I never in the mood, but I enjoy sex once we start?

blocks.x: A couple came to me wanting their intimacy back. I was explaining how long a woman's body can take to warm up, and I said it takes forty minutes. Four zero minutes, to be engorged enough to enjoy being penetrated, and to be juicy as fuck.
He said, “Oh yeah, don't have time for that.”
Her body answered before she did. Everything in her body language said: oh, ow. See, I'm not good enough here. I'm not quick enough.

He was wired to head straight for the finish line. She was much more energetic and much more sensual, and her way in takes longer. Two different bodies, and one of them had quietly decided it was the faulty one.
If you are never in the mood and then enjoy it once you start, your body may be asking for exactly that. A slower way in, and the time to take it.
Is it normal to be never in the mood but enjoy sex once started?
Yes. Wanting that only shows up once touch has begun is called responsive desire, and it is one of the normal ways desire works.
Where it comes from. In 2000 Rosemary Basson described a circular model of desire, drawn from research with women, in which closeness and touch can come first and the wanting grows out of them.
How common it is. Emily Nagoski's Come As You Are puts it at around three in ten women, and one in twenty men, whose desire is mainly responsive (about 30% and 5%).
When it shows up. It becomes more common once a relationship is past its first six to twelve months.
What it used to be called. The older model filed it as a desire disorder. Basson's model treats it as a normal variant.
So the pattern so many women type into a search bar as “low libido but enjoy sex” has a name, and the name describes a healthy body.
Why don't I want sex until we start?
Because a responsive body answers to what is happening, and before anything starts, nothing is happening yet for it to answer.
The other half of it is your way in. Just as there are love languages, every body has its own way into pleasure. I call it your Pleasure Language, and there are five.
Energetic. Eye contact, flirting across a room, the charge before anyone touches. Too much pressure, too fast, takes this body straight out.
Sensual. Smell, food, soft things, skin on skin. Dirty socks on the floor, a messy room or the thought “I didn't wash” can switch it off.
Sexual. Wired towards climax, and able to go from zero to a hundred very quickly.
Kinky. Anything that is taboo for you. That might be as simple as getting undressed with the lights on.
Shapeshifter. A bit of everything, and often starving when a partner only speaks one of the five.
If your partner goes straight for the genitals and your way in is energetic or sensual, of course your body stays quiet at the start, because it was never given its door.
I don't initiate, but I enjoy it. Is something wrong with me?
No. Not initiating tells you the order your desire arrives in, and it says nothing about how much you love your partner or how much pleasure your body can hold.
A responsive body rarely starts things, because the start is what it responds to. Once you stop reading that as a fault, you can stop apologising for it and start planning for it.
What helps when I'm never in the mood?
Stop waiting for the mood to come first, and plan the time and the touch your body warms up to. This is where I start couples.
Take sex off the table. Agree it out loud, so the touch has nowhere it has to go.
Schedule five minutes. No kids, no work, no phones. Five minutes is enough to begin.

Go back into your body. Remember when the two of you couldn't keep your hands off each other, and notice where in your body that memory lives. Often it is the hips, the lower back, the back of the heart.
Learn your way in. Find your Pleasure Language, so your partner knows whether to begin with your eyes, your skin, your senses or something a little taboo.
Give it the time it takes. If your body takes forty minutes, plan for forty minutes, and let the wanting arrive somewhere in the middle.

I go through all five Pleasure Languages in How Do We Find Our Way Into Pleasure?. If you want the research side laid out, What Is Responsive Desire, and Is It Normal? goes deeper, and Responsive vs Spontaneous Desire puts the two side by side.

Picture a year from now, still waiting for the mood to turn up before you let anyone close. Then picture five unhurried minutes where nothing has to happen, and your body gets to answer in its own time.

q: What do I do if my partner thinks intimacy cards are stupid or refuses to try them?

blocks.x: You found the cards. You felt hopeful for the first time in months. You showed him, and he said something like “we don't need a game to talk” and now you feel foolish for trying.
Here is what actually happened in that moment.

He did not reject the cards. He rejected the frame. When you hand a man a relationship tool, what his body often hears is: you think we are failing, and you think it is me. The no arrives before he has thought anything at all. It is a defence, and defences do not respond to better sales pitches.
The sideways way in

So stop announcing. Pick one question from the deck yourself. Ask it over dinner, in the car, on a walk. No deck on the table, no “I read that we should”, no frame at all. Just a genuinely curious question, asked once, received well.
Answer it yourself first if he hesitates. Going first is the move: it proves the water is safe.

A man left a comment on one of my reels that I have never forgotten. He had tried the cards with his daughter and found it easy. With his wife, impossible. “Why is it so easy with my daughter and not my wife?” The stakes were different. With his child he was not being graded. Your job is not to convince him the cards are good. It is to lower the stakes until the conversation stops feeling like an exam he might fail.
You do not need his yes to begin

One person changing the signal changes the system. I have watched this across more than 650 couples: when one partner stops pushing and starts asking one real question a week, receiving whatever comes back without correcting it, the other partner's resistance quietly runs out of things to defend against.
Weeks, sometimes. Faster than you would think, mostly. The man who said the cards were stupid is very often the man who, a month later, asks whose turn it is.
The deck can stay in the drawer while it does its first month of work. That is fine. It is working.

q: My partner has responsive desire. What do I do?

blocks.x: A hand on the shoulder while the dishwasher is being stacked. A lean in, wanting a little more.
She goes still. Something in her steps back, even though her feet don't move. She makes a joke, or remembers something that needs doing.
So you stand there with your hand cooling on the shoulder, wondering what the fuck you did. Is it me?
I tell that scene on my podcast with him as the one who goes still, and I say straight away that it runs both ways. Swap the pronouns in, whichever fit.
What I said there holds for her too. The step back almost never means she doesn't want her partner.
What does it mean to have a partner with responsive desire?
It means your partner's wanting usually arrives after touch and closeness have begun, so waiting for your partner to start can mean waiting for something that usually comes second.
The research. Rosemary Basson's work with women in 2000 drew desire as a loop, where touch and closeness can come before the wanting.
The numbers. Emily Nagoski's Come As You Are cites roughly 30% of women, against around 5% of men, as mainly responsive.
The timing. It shows up more once a couple is six to twelve months or more into the relationship.
The label. It is a normal variant of desire, for years misfiled as a disorder.
So if your wife never initiates sex, look at the order before you go looking for a reason.
Why does she never initiate?
Often because her desire is responsive, and a responsive body rarely starts things. It waits for something to respond to.

There can be a second layer. When reaching has usually come with a destination, her body learns that closeness arrives with a bill, and it braces before she has thought anything at all. A reflex, older than the two of them.
Your part in it is a loop the two of you have been running, and neither of you is the villain in it.
How do I help a partner with responsive desire?
Offer closeness with nothing on the end of it, read before you reach, and plan for the warming up. This is what I teach the men I work with.

Read before you reach. Ten seconds, three checks. Warm: is your partner's body warm and loose, or cool and held? Weight: settled, or perched and ready to move? Where: is the attention in the room with you, or already somewhere else?
Give something with no ask inside. If your partner is cool, perched and somewhere else, that is the moment to stay close, say nothing, and let your presence be felt.
Take sex off the table for a while. Say it out loud, so a touch can land and go nowhere.
Plan for warm-up time. A responsive body can take forty minutes or more to be ready. If you only ever leave five, you are asking for the wanting before it can arrive.
Ask instead of guessing. “Are you present enough for me to touch you right now?” is a whole check-in in one line.
I go further into the brace and the bill in Why Does He Pull Away the Moment You Get Close?, and into the different ways people find their way into pleasure in How Do We Find Our Way Into Pleasure?.
How do I create desire in a partner with responsive desire?
Desire in a responsive body answers to conditions, so build the conditions and let the wanting come in its own order.
So often it only takes one person in a couple wanting to make the change for the whole pattern to start moving.
If that person is you, start with your own reach. Keep landing the same hand in the same place, asking for nothing, and give it the weeks it takes to trust that this one is going nowhere.

If the closeness has already gone quiet between the two of you, Why Does She Go Quiet? is the place to start, and Why Am I Never in the Mood, but I Enjoy Sex Once We Start? is the same pattern told from the other side of the bed.

Picture another year of reaching, waiting to be reached for first, and reading the stillness as a no. Then picture a hand that lands, asks for nothing, and lifts away, and what a body that has been waiting for exactly that might do next.

q: How do couples rebuild desire after a long dry spell?

blocks.x: In one exercise I teach, one person makes offers and the other answers no. Would you like a cup of tea? No. Would you like the window open? No. Two minutes of nothing but no, and then you notice where that no lives in your body.

Round two flips it. Every offer is an easy yes, and you do not follow through on any offer. I teach this in my couples VIP days and in my couples work, with clothes on and in daylight, because a long gap can teach a body that every yes is a promise. The game hands yes and no back to you as something small and safe to practise.
Why doesn't desire come back by itself after a long dry spell?

Because after a long gap every reach becomes a question the body answers before you do. In my work that answer is often a brace, a tightening that arrives before anyone has decided anything. You can both be bracing at the same moment from opposite directions, and neither of you is the villain in it.

The reach itself can read as a demand. Closeness has come with a bill before, a next step or a big talk, so your body keeps its distance, because distance feels survivable. A sentence like "I miss you" can land in a braced body as "I am not enough". That reflex is older than the relationship, and it says nothing about whether you are wanted. I explain the other side of it in my episode on why he pulls away the moment you get close.
What should we do first after a long gap?
Start with something so small that neither of you can fail at it. In order:

Each of you does Touch Base® alone, twice a day. Thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say "I am safe right now", hold for two minutes. If that means locking yourself in the loo to get the two minutes, you do it.

Play the offers game. Two minutes of no, two minutes of easy yeses, then two minutes where you answer yes or no exactly as you feel it. Nobody follows through on any offer. Afterwards ask each other what it was like to receive an offer you did not have to act on.
Read the room for ten seconds before you reach. Is the body warm and loose, or cool and held? Settled, or perched and ready to move? Is the attention in the room with you, or already somewhere else?
I go through the skills behind the offers game in the episode on the skill you practise alone.
What can I give my partner that asks for nothing back?

Your presence, with no ask inside it. If your partner is cool and perched, that is the moment to give something, not to reach for something. Sit near your partner, say nothing, and let the room fill with someone close who wants nothing and is fully there. Your nervous system starts to calibrate your partner's.
I teach this to the men I work with as well. Closeness with no next step attached is something neither of you may have had for a long time, and it is where a braced body starts to thaw.
Will a date night or a weekend away fix it?

Rarely, if the body is still bracing underneath. More effort and more atmosphere go into the evening while the body stays shut. I dig into that in the episode on booking the date night and still feeling nothing.

If you already know what would help and still cannot start, I have written that answer out in full. Everything I do is at Feel Fully You, and the quickest way in is the Touch Reset Quiz, which names the stage you are in.
A dry spell is a pattern, and patterns can be changed. It starts with one small thing both bodies can say yes to.

q: How do you rebuild physical intimacy in a long relationship without pressure?

blocks.x: Your bedroom has no edges. There is no green light to start, no end, and no way to say not tonight without it turning into a conversation about the state of the relationship. Every reach could be nothing, or it could be everything, so your body prepares for everything, every single time.
That is where the pressure lives: in the missing container. It does not mean you are cold, and it does not mean your partner is doing it wrong. A nervous system with no information does exactly this.
What is a container for touch?

A container is an agreement you both make before touch begins. I learned it in the room where I worked as a dominatrix, and I teach it today in my VIP days. Before anything starts, you agree on the edges together:
What is on, what is off, and what is a hard no.
Where you would like to expand a little, and what you want to learn.
How long it lasts, because a body that knows when something stops can relax inside it.
A stoplight for the middle. Red means everything stops. Orange or yellow means slow down, take a breath and anchor, because that is where the growth is. Green means keep going.

The no is heard the first time. In my experience, bodies open faster inside a container like this than inside anything else I have worked with. The leather and the flogger have nothing to do with it, those are sensory extras. The container is the start, the end, the no and the yes.
The story of that room is in my episode what a dungeon taught me about your bedroom.
How do we try touch without pressure tonight?
Ask for two minutes with no agenda. Here is the version I teach first:
Ask out loud. One of you says, "Can I trace your face for two minutes?" Agree that it is two minutes, no more.
Divide the roles. One gives and one only receives. This touch is not going anywhere, and you can both say so.
Soften the jaw. Close your eyes if you can. Let the urge to smile or to hurry it along pass.
Trace with the lightest contact you can. Start just under the ear, where the little knob sticks out, and follow the jaw. Notice where your breath catches.
Give it one word. No sentence and no story. Then say thank you.

Some of you will feel warmth or a buzz under the skin, and some will feel nothing. Nothing is information. A quiet body is a body that stopped believing touch was going to be worthwhile, and two minutes at a time is how that belief changes.
Why does touch from a stranger feel easier than touch from my partner?

Because a stranger asks nothing from you. You know that touch is not going to lead to sex, so nothing is at stake and you are not trying to predict where it ends. I wrote up that answer in why you can feel it with someone else but not the man you love, and you can hear it in my podcast episode on it. A container gives your partner the same gift: touch that asks for nothing.

If touch with your partner always ends up in the same place, I have written about that too, in why touch always leads to sex. You can see everything I do as an intimacy and touch coach in the UK at Feel Fully You, and the Touch Reset Quiz is the quickest way in.
Pressure falls away when your body knows the edges. Give it a start, an end and a no that is heard.

q: How do couples reconnect after years of distance?

blocks.x: Before I ask a couple to talk, I ask them to notice where the missing thing lives in the body.
A hollowness? An emptiness? A bit of sadness? The ache of remembering when you could not keep your hands off each other?
That is where I start, with sex taken off the table. Years of distance do not arrive in a night, so a big conversation will not close them in one either.
Can a couple really reconnect after years of distance?
Yes, and it often starts with one person wanting the change. You have both grown and changed since the early days, and that is perfectly okay. It does not mean things have to stay as they are.

I see it often with the couples I work with. A few years go by, and you become bed partners, roommates, sometimes in different rooms. You deeply love each other and something feels like it is missing.
Then comes the line I hear again and again: he doesn't want to change, she doesn't want to change. Nobody wants to be told what they are doing wrong, or to be fixed. So I start somewhere else.
Why do couples drift apart for years without noticing?

It builds in small moments, not in one big one. A reach lands wrong. One of you goes still, the other reads the stillness as rejection and stops reaching, and the stopping looks like proof that going still was right. Neither of you is reaching any more, and nobody has named it.

Stress piles on top. Long working days, the children, a partner who is exhausted. Phones, laptops and the television eat a great deal of attention too. In the beginning there was exquisite attention on you from your lover. Now that feeling of being read can seem like too much, even though you once loved it.
Where do we start when we have been apart this long?
Start small, in this order:
Take sex off the table for now. Make that decision out loud, together.
Schedule five minutes. No children, no work, no phones. Remember what it felt like to be read by each other, and notice where in your body that memory lands.
Begin Touch Base on your own. Thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say "I am safe right now", and hold for two minutes.
Protect a date morning. Forty-five to ninety minutes beats a tired date night. Both of you clean and juicy, one person sets up a tidy room, the music is on, and you use structured communication.
Add the cards. Fifteen minutes a week with a card from the Intimacy and Communication Cards.
For a daily rhythm, 31 Days Closer gives you one card a day, already in order.
What if only one of us wants to change?
Then that one starts, and the start is with yourself. Leave your partner's part out of it for now. The question I give is: what do I need right now to feel even more safe?
Touch Base is where that begins. Once your body has been shown that it is safe, desire can come back again, and from there it can be super hot.

If the distance has a story behind it that feels bigger than reconnecting, my answer on a marriage that went cold goes into the three stages, and I talk through the quiet, the brace and the gone in Season 2, episode 33 of the podcast. For the five-minute exercise in my own voice, listen to episode 94.
You can see everything I do at Feel Fully You, where I work as an intimacy and touch coach in the UK, and if you want me alongside you, The Beginning is my three-month programme for couples.
Five minutes with the phones in another room, and one honest answer, is a real place to begin.

Notice the held breath. It is the window before the brace shows.

A body tracks the body beside it faster than the mind catches up. I wrote the full field guide in What Her Body Is Telling You.

They laughed. “That’s what we’re here for with you.” Three months later they went on a second honeymoon.

What actually happens during relationship coaching?
We find the loop, we take it out of your bodies so you can both see it, and then we give you a structure to practise something new inside.

Find the loop. Say its shape out loud, with no blame and no names in it. "You reach, I brace. You pull back, I feel alone." Most people feel something in the chest drop about half an inch the first time they hear it said as a shape.

How do I know if I need relationship coaching?

The date night got booked, the food was gorgeous, and the drive home still felt empty.

A hand lands on a back and a body tightens, before anyone has decided anything.
