q: Responsive vs spontaneous desire: what is the difference?

blocks.x: He got the sitter. You shaved your legs in the shower. The place had the good lighting, and the fish was absolutely scrumptious.

You sat down across from him wanting to feel something. The wine came, the starter came. Your body stayed exactly where it had been all week. Shut. Polite. A slight tightness in the jaw, in the neck, in the shoulders.
Then the drive home, and backs turned to each other in bed.

I talk about that evening in You Booked the Date Night and Still Felt Nothing, because so many of you have lived it. The whole plan rests on one story about desire: if it were right, it would just arrive. That story describes one of the two types of desire. For a lot of bodies, the wanting runs the other way round.
What is spontaneous desire?
Spontaneous desire is wanting that arrives before anything has happened. A thought, a glance, and the wanting is already there.
It is the version most of us were taught. For a long time it was treated as the only real kind, so anyone whose wanting did not arrive that way assumed something had gone wrong with them.
What does responsive desire mean?
Responsive desire means the wanting arrives second. Touch comes first, or closeness, or the right context, and desire grows out of what is already underway.
I call this your Desire Style. It is the order the wanting arrives in, and it sits alongside your Touch Pattern and your Pleasure Language as one of the ways you are wired.
Safety is the switch that turns it back on. Once your body has been shown that it is safe, desire can come back again.
Responsive desire vs spontaneous desire: how do they compare?
They differ in what comes first, and in what waiting does to you.

Rosemary Basson first documented the reversed order in 2000, from research with women, in a circular model where closeness and stimulation can come before the wanting. Emily Nagoski carried it into the mainstream with Come As You Are, and the figure she cites is roughly 30% of women and about 5% of men running mainly responsive, with responsive desire becoming more common after the first six to twelve months of a relationship. For decades a body that wanted second was filed under a disorder, and Basson’s model places it where it belongs, as a normal variant of how desire works.
Which type of desire do I have?
You can usually tell by what happens when you wait. Notice which of these sounds like you.
You rarely think about sex out of nowhere, and you enjoy it once it has started. That leans responsive.
A thought or a glance is enough to get you wanting. That leans spontaneous.

Your wanting used to arrive on its own and now turns up later, after closeness. That shift is common after the early months of a relationship, and expected for a lot of bodies in their 40s, 50s and 60s.
None of these is better. Each one simply tells you which door to use.
What do I do if my desire is responsive?
Stop waiting to feel like it first, and set up the conditions the wanting can follow. This is the order I teach.
Touch Base® first. Thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say “I am safe right now”, and hold for two minutes.
Swap the date night for a date morning. At the end of the night you are tired. Plan between 45 and 90 minutes earlier in the day.
Set up the room. Both of you clean. One person gets the room ready, tidy, with the music out.
Start with touch that has no destination. The only job is to feel safe.
Let the wanting arrive in its own order. When your body knows it is safe and it turns hot, go for it.
Desire only comes to a body that trusts its no will be honoured. I wrote about that in The Body Does Not Open on Command. If your wanting has gone quieter with menopause, this answer goes further.
Picture another year of booking the table and waiting for the wanting to arrive first. Then picture one slow morning where the touch comes first, and you let your body answer.

q: How do couples in a sexless marriage reconnect physically?

Three months after they started, they went on a second honeymoon.
Six weeks earlier I had told them sex was off the table. They laughed at me. “That’s what we came to you for!” Here is why it worked.
Why does a marriage become sexless?
Most couples focus on the wrong thing. They focus on the sex.

What I see, over and over, is two people who love each other and have stopped having fun. Somewhere along the way they started living like roommates. They run the house, they run the diary, they are kind to each other. They just don’t touch. They don’t talk about it either.
The sex went quiet because the play went first.
What do couples get wrong when they try to fix it?
They have the one big talk
When they do talk about it, it becomes ONE big conversation. It always drags up a lot of old stuff. Blaming. Shaming. Who stopped reaching first, and when, and why.
It pulls them further apart. Then nobody wants to raise it again for another year.
They book a weekend away
Or they book a tantra session, or a weekend away, thinking that if only they had more time and a place away from it all, they would connect again.
They won’t.
A weekend away can be gorgeous. Then you come home on Sunday night and the way you live together is exactly where you left it.
How do you get physical intimacy back in a marriage?
With small, regular, structured touch and talk, at home, inside a container. This is the order I work in.
Take sex off the table

When you take sex off the table, you can reconnect again. Every touch stops being a question. Nobody is bracing for where it might lead, nobody is scanning for the tiger in the background… so the body can actually feel the hand that is on it.
Focus on what is going well

The 23-year couple had been so focused on what wasn’t working that it was all they were getting. So their first exercises were about what WAS going well between them, and everything they used to love about each other.
Touch dates, on a timer, with no sex

Structured physical and emotional touch dates, without any sex. They start short and grow as the body says yes. The timer is the container: you know when it starts and you know when it ends, so you can relax into the middle.
Communication prompts, in place of the big talk

One prompt at a time, using my Intimacy and Communication Cards and the Dyad. One of you speaks. The other only answers with one of three things: thank you, clarify that, or summarise that. Then you swap.
Try one today. Here’s a free card from the couples deck: “Tell me something I need to know about you and your body.” Take turns. Say thank you. Leave it there… no fixing, no debate.

Couples who still love each other and want each other back. Straight couples, same-sex couples and LGBTQ+ couples. I work with all of them.

Many of my couples are over 40. If there are erection changes, or menopause is changing things, we work it out together. Couples where I notice abuse. I name it straight away.
Couples where one person believes the other is the only one to blame.

q: What does it mean when she says she's fine but her whole body changes?

blocks.x: She says fine. The smile does not reach her eyes. The yes came a fraction of a second too fast, and her shoulders, which had begun to soften, came back up.
Her body voted no while her mouth voted yes.

This is the override, and it is one of the most misread signals in every relationship I have worked with. A woman raised inside a family, a culture, a body that learned her clear no creates consequences has practised overriding for decades. By the time she met you it was automatic. She barely notices it herself.
Why asking makes it deepen

Most men, suspecting something, ask: are you sure you are okay? She says yes. The override deepens. Six days or six months later something erupts that seems to come from nowhere, and you are accused of missing what you were never shown.
She does not need you to interrogate her. She needs you to make the room safer than the override.
What that looks like

Staying steady when something difficult is finally named. Keeping your hurt out of her disclosure. Letting her feelings surface without making the conversation about yours. Each time you manage that, her body files a new piece of evidence. The body learns slowly because it has been collecting the old evidence for a long time. The data point matters more than the conversation.

One couple I worked with: a senior partner at a law firm, brilliant at solving things, and a wife who had been overriding for thirty-one years. Three months in she said, I had no idea there was this much of me underneath it. He stopped being a system she had to manage. She returned to herself.
Twenty-seven years of watching what bodies do when nobody is performing. The override is the first thing I look for.

q: We sleep in the same bed but never touch anymore. What happened?

blocks.x: You go to bed. Backs towards each other. One of you scrolls, one of you is already pretending to sleep, and the space between you has become a thing you both know how to lie next to.
I hear this one from couples all the time. They are kind to each other. They share a bed, a kettle and a diary. Nobody can point to the day it stopped.
What actually happened when we stopped touching?
Usually nothing dramatic happened. Touch went flat first, because life got loud and you both stopped reaching.

I call this the quiet. Nothing is wrong, exactly. You are busy, you are tired, and the small touches that used to happen on the way past each other just stopped being part of the day. The longer it runs, the more reaching starts to feel like a decision instead of a habit.

If this is where you are, the way back is gentler than you think. I teach couples to plan a date morning rather than a date night, because by the end of the evening you are tired. Forty-five to ninety minutes, both of you clean and juicy, one person sets up the room, tidy, music on, and a structure for talking so that nobody has to guess.
Why does my body tighten when my partner reaches for me?
Because the tightening happens before you decide anything. I call it the brace.

A hand lands on your back. Before you have thought a single thought, your body has already tightened. You override it. You let the hand stay, maybe it moves on to something else. But the brace has happened underneath the thought, and it is often not about what your partner just did. It can go back much earlier than this relationship.

It works the same way in men. If you are the one who braces when your partner approaches, you are not alone either. A date night on top of the brace does not move much, because the brace was never about the restaurant.
What is the roommate stage, and is it the end?
The roommate stage is what I call the gone, and it is not the end. You stop bracing because you stopped expecting.

People living side by side. Perfectly kind, and away. Some bracing is still in there, and some blame: blame for yourself, blame for the other person, a resentment that starts to arrive. Under it sits a quiet thought that this is what life is going to be like now.

I have watched couples in exactly this place start touching again. One couple had not made love in 23 years, and I tell their story on the sexless marriage page. Three months into a structure, they were. I am not shocked by any of this any more.
Why did the date night not fix it?
Because most couples are in the brace or the gone, and a date night is the fix for the quiet.

The usual story is that desire arrives by itself if the setting is right. Candles, a weekend away, a tantra workshop, nicer underwear. Spontaneity is the lie. It is the reason you keep booking the restaurant and the drive home feels empty.

More effort and more things, without changing anything underneath, only add more input to a body that is already guarded. Your body reads all of it as one more thing to manage. You were using the fix for a different stage, and that is all. Our intimacy and communication cards, over 150 cards in the app, give you a gentler container for the quiet and the brace, one card and three answers at a time.
What can I do tonight, on my own?
Start with Touch Base. It takes two minutes and nobody else needs to be in the room.
Put your thumb to your forefinger.
Move slowly and feel the ridges.
Say out loud, "I am safe right now."
Hold for two minutes.

Do it in the car, in the loo, in bed. You may yawn, your tummy may gurgle, or a tension you have carried all day may start to let go. It is two minutes of touch with no destination. The only point is to feel safe, and that is what brings you back into connection with yourself first, before any touch between the two of you.

I learned this from my own body first. For years I gave and gave and felt nothing come back in a form I could receive, my jaw clenched and my breath high, until my body stopped asking politely. I talk about it in episode 36 of The Scrumptious Woman, and about my own marriage in episode 33.
If you want company on this, I am Feel Fully You, and working with couples one to one is what I do. The Beginning is the deepest way in.
You love your partner, and your body can still stay shut. Both are true at the same time, and both can change.

q: What is a somatic coach, and is there one in the UK for intimacy?

blocks.x: There is a wasp in the room while I am recording. I get up, try to close the window, hunt for it, tell myself it is fine.

Then I notice a tightening in my chest. A tightening in my hips and my sacrum. I make my out breath longer than my in breath, and it clicks: I was in a little bit of a freeze, and I had skipped straight over it.
That is the subtlety of embodiment, and I told that story on my podcast about Somatic Experiencing. A somatic coach teaches you to catch it, and intimacy and touch is where I use it most.
What does a somatic coach actually do?
A somatic coach tracks what is happening in your body and helps it move what it has been holding. With me it looks like this.
We track the sensation. Take a breath and scan: are you open or contracted? Tense, or loose?
We find the edge of it. Where does the tightness start, and where does it stop?
We stay with it. Long enough for your body to begin letting go of the charge it has been holding.
We move it through. Breath, tremoring, movement. Your body comes down before you decide anything.
On my podcast I said it plainly: it’s never good to take a lot of action from that space. Your body needs to come down first.
Good news needs this too. Your nervous system is often quite okay holding on to the hard things. Receiving something good is when your system can blow out, so even joy gets a little calibration.

Yes. I live in England and work in person and online, so anywhere in the UK works, and further. Here is where people tend to begin with Feel Fully You.
Picture another year of overriding what your body is telling you. Then picture trusting it.

q: How do I support a partner who has trauma around touch?

blocks.x: My subconscious buried my date rape for over 25 years. It came back when I was in a BDSM class and my body started shaking, and then my body actually did something about it. I tell you this because a partner with sexual trauma may not have the story to give you yet. The body often goes first, and the memory follows.

Most of the women and couples I work with come to feel safe enough, and once that happens they remember what happened to them. Then they work through it together. So the most useful offering comes before any technique: a body that is safe enough to remember.
What does my partner’s flinch actually mean?

A partner’s body is protecting them, and the protection started long before anyone arrived. My definition of trauma is anything that happened too soon or too fast for the psyche or body to absorb, and that leaves an imprint.
So a flinch can come from a story a partner has told, a story they have told nobody, or one their mind cannot reach yet. The reflex looks the same from the outside.

I talk about the slightly braced, slightly gone feeling from the inside in episode 33 of The Scrumptious Woman. If the freeze is the part that worries you, why do I freeze when my partner touches me goes further into it.
How do I support a partner with trauma, whether we are dating or years into a marriage?

Build safety first, in pieces a partner can say yes to. Dating someone with trauma or a long way into a marriage, the order is the same, and safety is the first thing I build with every client, before desire and before any technique.
Start with your own body. Touch Base: thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say “I am safe right now”, and hold for two minutes.
Offer it, never insist. Touch Base can be learned in a partner’s own time, on their own, with no touch attached.
Ask before any touch. The intimacy and communication cards, over 150 cards in the app, give the question a home, so asking becomes a habit rather than a negotiation.
Keep it short. For someone with trauma, being still and slow can bring up more tightness, so a short practice done often beats a long one done once.
Nothing happens to a partner’s body without a yes from that partner. I teach women their no, and what their no lives in: their body.
Should we wait until my partner has healed?

No, because waiting until the healing is done is one of the quieter stories couples tell themselves. “We will do it when I have dealt with my trauma, when you have dealt with yours.” The story keeps the power to change things sitting somewhere else, where nobody has to pick it up.
Small contained touch, offered with a clear yes, builds the safety that healing needs. I describe the quiet story in episode 38.
What if a memory comes back while we are being close?
Stay, and let the body do what it is doing. The only way to move through an experience is to feel it, and a body that starts to shake or cry or go quiet is moving through it.

You do not need to explain it, fix it or fill the silence. This is also the point where I would rather you had a guide than went it alone. Couples do this work with me together, and The Beginning, my three month couples intensive, is where that happens.
Where do we go for more help?

Start with the step that matches who is reading. If you are the partner, my free guide When She Goes Quiet is written for men who love someone and cannot find the door back in. If your partner wants to look at it from the other side, the Touch Reset Quiz is a gentle first step.

Your partner’s body is not asking for a fix. It is asking to be safe enough to remember.

q: Why do I cringe when my partner touches me because it always leads to sex?

blocks.x: He reaches for your hand at the table and your stomach tightens before you've thought a single thing. You want him near you. Your body has learned something separate: that his hand rarely stays just a hand. It's the opening line of a conversation that's going to end up somewhere specific, and you feel cornered before it's even begun.

This is a different pattern from going numb or feeling nothing. You feel plenty. What you feel is trapped, because touch stopped being able to just be touch. It became a request, every time, and your body started answering the request before you'd consciously registered it was being made.
Why "just say no" doesn't fix this

The obvious advice is to simply say no when you don't want it to go further. That's true, and it doesn't touch the actual pattern, because the bracing happens before the choice point, at the first touch, not at the moment things escalate. Saying no after you've already flinched at hello doesn't rebuild the thing that broke. What rebuilds it is touch that reliably, provably, does not lead anywhere else, often enough that your body stops needing to defend against the possibility.
What separating touch from sex actually looks like

This is the whole logic behind structured, non-sexual touch: a defined block of time, an obvious end, and an agreement, held by both of you, that this specific touch goes nowhere else tonight. Not forever. Just enough times, with an outcome your body can verify for itself, that touch stops being a euphemism and starts being allowed to be only what it is.

You can say this out loud tonight, before either of you buys anything: "Five minutes, my hand on your arm, and it ends there. If either of us wants more, we say so out loud, we don't just drift there." Naming the edge, in words, before the touch starts, is what lets your body actually rest inside it instead of scanning for where it's headed.

Trust that touch means only what it says is rebuilt one honoured boundary at a time, not one conversation.

q: Why do I flinch or freeze when my partner touches me, even though I trust him?

blocks.x: He runs a hand along your arm, gentle, the way he always does, and your whole body locks. Or the room gets far away, his voice arriving from another floor, and you come back a few seconds later without fully knowing where you went. That locking has a name: the freeze response during intimacy.

You already know it has nothing to do with him, and knowing hasn't changed a thing, because the part of you reacting is running a much older instruction: a body that learned, somewhere, that a hand arriving could mean danger, and it built a reflex faster than thought to protect you from it. That reflex doesn't check the calendar. It doesn't know this is a man who has never hurt you. It just fires.
Why do I go still when touched, even by someone I love?

Because your body has practised overriding its own no for a long time, often since you were small. Think back to being three or four, when a relative came to the house and you were sent over for a hug. Everything in your body was pulling back. You did it anyway, because it was expected of you.

I see this in parents, in my couples, and in the coaches I mentor who carry trauma, something that happened too soon, too fast. Often it is sexual, because that is what brings people to me. Often it is other kinds of trauma too.

Sometimes it is smaller. A look that landed in your body and did not feel good. A hand that grazed your leg on the tube. You froze, and you said nothing. Each of those moments told your body that your no could be overridden, so now, when a hand arrives, your body goes still before you have decided anything.

Teaching women where their no lives, in their body, is the part of my work as an intimacy and touch coach in the UK that matters most to me. I talk it through on the podcast in The Power of Saying No.
Seven days, fifteen minutes a day, my voice guiding every one. Just you and your own hands, so your body leads and you decide how far each day goes.
Is freezing during sex the same as the fawn response in relationships?

They are closely related: freezing is going still, and fawning is saying yes while your body is saying no. Your partner comes in for a kiss, it does not feel nice, and you go ahead anyway. Afterwards comes the shame spiral, the beating yourself up about it.
A simple exercise. Not an easy one.
Look back at this week. Where did you say no? Where did a yes come out of your mouth while your body was bracing?
Notice without judging. Every one of those moments is information.
Practise one small adjustment out loud. "Hey darling, I'd love a kiss, and at the moment I'm not feeling it. How about we connect when I'm done for the day?"
Drop the explanation. A no does not always need one.
If the room goes far away instead of going still, there is a separate page on dissociating during sex.
Why doesn't understanding my freeze make it stop?

Because understanding a reflex and retraining a reflex are two entirely different jobs, and the second one happens through the body. You can probably explain exactly why this happens. You've named the pattern, understood the mechanism from every angle available to you. You still flinch.
What actually retrains a freeze response?

The work here is to give your body so many small, predictable, low-stakes experiences of touch that its prediction slowly updates: this hand, at this speed, in this size, does not mean what the old one meant. Every rep counts. None can be rushed to look like progress.

Start entirely alone. Touch Base®: thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say to yourself "I am safe right now", and hold for two minutes. This part is just for you, teaching your own nervous system, on your own schedule, what safe contact feels like when nothing is being asked of you in return. If you want me to guide you through the next steps on your own, One Touch is seven days of guided self-touch, built for exactly this. If you freeze during intimacy and your partner takes it personally, this is the next step. When you're ready to bring him into it, one prompt with three allowed responses (the Dyad: "Thank you," "Clarify that," "Summarise that") lets you tell him what you need without either of you having to guess or defend.
If you want to work on this with me one to one, a VIP day is where we go deepest.
A reflex that took a long time to build needs new evidence, delivered slowly enough for your body to actually believe it.

q: How to enjoy touch again when it started to feel like a chore

blocks.x: In the last few weeks, speaking at an event and co-leading a retreat, four women came up to me with almost the same sentence. They had tried a touch exercise on the inside of the wrist and felt nothing. Each one had decided there was something wrong with her.
I told each of them to take a breath. What they described is absolutely normal.
Why does touch start to feel like a chore?
Touch starts to feel like a chore when it becomes a job to get right, because a body that is being audited stops answering.

A chore has an outcome. It is done for someone else, it has a standard, and it ends when it is finished. Touch that arrives with "am I doing this right?" and "should I be feeling more?" has the same shape. You end up looking at the ceiling, running the clock in your head and checking a face.
What does the research say about enjoying touch?
A study from a team in Essex, which I cover in episode 47 of The Scrumptious Woman, found that body awareness is three separate skills doing three different jobs.

Noticing gets you there, and trusting makes it worth arriving. Both are about listening, and a chore leaves no room for that. Attention regulation is the one that gets trained most, and it stayed with solo sex. It did not travel into the room with a partner.
That is why so many women practise alone for years, get good at it, and then conclude the fault is theirs. They were handed half an instruction.
How do you enjoy touch again when it has started to feel like a chore?
Take the wrist. It takes about three minutes, and the whole job is to ask one question: is that a yes?
Turn one hand palm up and find the soft patch on the inside of the wrist.
Stroke it with two fingers of the other hand and ask: is that a yes?
Change direction and ask again.
Go lighter, almost grazing, as if the hairs on the wrist might lift. Ask again.
Add your nails, down and then up. Ask again.
Watch your own hand, then close your eyes. Notice whether either one changes the sensation.

Whether it is nice and whether you ought to feel it are two other questions, and you can leave both at the door. You will probably have no idea in the first minute, and saying so is the honest answer. What you are building is capacity and curiosity, and the difficulty is the sign the exercise is working.
How do we bring a partner into it without it becoming another task?
Use offers and requests, where nothing gets done. It runs in three rounds of about two minutes, and nobody follows through on any of it.
Every answer is no. One of you offers ("Would you like a cup of tea?"), and the other says no to everything. Notice where in your body the no settles. No is a full sentence.
Every answer is yes. The offers are easy ones, like playing with your hair. The other person receives the yes, and nothing happens next.
Say whichever is true. The offers come, and you answer yes or no exactly as you feel it.

Afterwards, notice whether it was easier to ask or to say yes. I run this in my couples work, and I teach it so that touch stays a question. A yes you can feel is information, and information is what a chore never gives you.

If you want somewhere gentle to start on your own, One Touch is seven days of guided self-touch for learning to feel your own body again. I am an intimacy and touch coach in the UK, and why you may not feel anything when your partner touches you goes further into the same pattern.
Touch stops being a chore the moment your body gets to answer.

q: Why can't I stand to be touched after having a baby?

blocks.x: You put her down for the night and your skin is still ringing with the day. Small hands. A mouth. A weight against you for hours on end. He reaches for your shoulder and you flinch like he's a stranger. You love him. You still cannot stand one more hand on you tonight.

There is a sentence worth saying out loud, because it is true. It's not you, it's me. Not as an apology. As physiology. A body that has given itself to another person's needs all day has a limit, and that limit fills before the day is over. This is not about him. It is not about desire dying. It is a nervous system running a deficit, and touch, any touch, reads as one more withdrawal it cannot currently afford.
Why this is not a relationship pattern

The instinct is to read this as proof something has gone wrong between you. It hasn't. A newborn is not a small addition to your day, she is the whole architecture of it, and your body has been on duty since the last time it slept properly. Being touched out is what a body does when it has already given everything it has to someone else first. It is common, and it moves, and it has nothing to do with how much you want him.
The reach that actually works here

What he can offer right now is not more touch. It is touch with an edge: a start and a clear end, so no part of you has to brace for it becoming something bigger. And what you can offer yourself is a way back into your own body that asks nothing of anyone. Touch Base®: thumb pressed to forefinger, moved slow, like melted chocolate, no rushing. Say to yourself, I am safe right now. Keep going for two minutes, on your own, whenever the day allows it. It rebuilds your own relationship with touch before it has to be shared with anyone else again.
This capacity refills, on its own timeline. Respecting that timeline is not indulgence. It is what lets it refill faster.

The five languages

Your state answers first, whether a braced body files it under interruption or a present body lets it arrive. Your language answers next, whether that kiss is food or noise. Your pattern has the final word, whether you receive it, brace against it, or start planning what to give back. Same kiss, five seconds, three things deciding what happens next.

q: What is responsive desire, and is it normal?

blocks.x: Responsive desire is wanting that arrives after touch or closeness has begun, rather than before it, and it is normal. Juliette Karaman, an intimacy and touch expert in the UK, works with it by giving it a container.
Say the word structure to most women and something in them goes tight. It sounds like admin. It sounds like the opposite of being wanted.
Say the word dominatrix to the same woman and she leans in.

I worked as a dominatrix, and that room taught me more about responsive desire than almost anything else. Before anything began, two people agreed. What’s on, what’s off, what’s a hard no, how long it lasts. With that container in place, bodies opened faster than in anything else I have worked in.

Then take that home for a second. A bedroom with no edges. No start, no end, no way to say “not now” without it turning into a whole conversation about the state of the relationship. Every reach could be nothing or it could be everything… so the body prepares for everything. Every single time.
What is responsive desire?
Responsive desire is wanting that shows up once something has already started. Touch, closeness or the right setting comes first, and desire builds out of that.

So if you have ever said “I never feel like sex until we start”, you have described responsive desire almost word for word. Its opposite, spontaneous desire, arrives first, out of a thought. I put the two side by side in Responsive vs Spontaneous Desire.
If this is you, never being in the mood but enjoying it once you start is the same pattern. If this is your partner, here is what to do when your partner has responsive desire.
Is responsive desire normal?
Yes, responsive desire is normal, and the research has said so since 2000.
Rosemary Basson, 2000. Working from women’s own experience, she drew desire as a circle, where closeness and stimulation can come before the wanting.
Emily Nagoski, Come As You Are. She brought it to a wide audience and cites roughly 30% of women and about 5% of men as mainly responsive.
Time together. Responsive desire becomes more common after the first six to twelve months of a relationship.
The old label. A body that wanted second used to be filed under a desire disorder, and Basson’s model places it as a normal variant.

For many women in their 40s, 50s and 60s, desire moves towards the responsive end, and that shift is expected.

The wanting that used to arrive on its own starts turning up later, after the touch has begun. A lot of women read that as a loss, when what has changed is the order. If that is happening alongside menopause, this answer goes into the body side of it.

Give it a container, so your body knows what is happening before the touch begins. This is the dungeon, scaled all the way down and taken home.
Agree before anything starts. What’s on, what’s off, what’s a no.
Agree how long. Once your body knows how long something lasts, it can relax and stay.
Use a stoplight. Green, keep going. Orange, slow down and take a breath, this is where the growth is. Red, everything stops.
Let a no be heard the first time. That is what lets your body stop preparing for everything.
Curiosity instead of a goal. The touch is going nowhere. Notice what your body does once it knows that.

It sounds hella unjuicy. It is also how your body starts to explore, and once you have done two or three minutes of it you can start expanding the capacity. q: My husband hates being touched, even by me. How do I improve our intimacy without crossing his limits?

Why reaching more makes it worse

The instinct, when someone you love pulls away, is to close the gap. Reach again, more gently, more often, hoping persistence reads as safety. It closes by him experiencing enough small, unpressured, exitable moments of touch that his body updates what touch actually costs.
What actually respects his limits and still moves things

Structure helps here more than warmth does, because structure gives him something warmth can't: a guaranteed end. A touch with a defined stop, agreed in advance, that neither of you have to negotiate in the moment, is the single easiest way to lower the stakes enough for his body to try it. Ask, out loud, for something absurdly small and completely time-boxed. Thirty seconds of his hand in yours, an agreed stop, no expectation of more. Let him choose the moment. Let him end it.

Pick a single question, said out loud in capitals: "TELL ME WHAT TOUCH FEELS LIKE TO YOUR BODY RIGHT NOW." He answers, fully and honestly. You may only say "Thank you," "Clarify that," or "Summarise that," nothing else, no fixing, no defending what you hear. Then it's your turn on the same prompt. It gets you real information without either of you having to survive an argument to get it.
His limit is not a rejection of you. It's data about what his body can currently verify as safe, and data like that changes with evidence, not with wanting it to.

Knowing is never what stands in the way. I explain why the body freezes in this episode of my podcast.

The stage decides the fix, and most couples apply the fix for the wrong one. I talk about three stages on the date night episode:
Most couples are in the brace or the gone and keep applying the fix for the quiet. That does not mean you failed. It means the stage was misread.
Do I need a relationship coach or a personal growth coach?

Choose by who is willing to start. If your partner is in, a relationship coach who works through the body and touch fits, and The Beginning is where couples start. If you are on your own, begin with One Touch, which is seven days of structured self-touch.

Why does effort alone stop working?

Because a candlelit evening or a weekend away adds sensation, and the stage you are in needs safety. Spontaneity is the lie. The nervous system opens when it knows what happens next, and a clear start and a clear end give it that.
If you want to see how that looks in practice, an intimacy and touch coach in the UK can show you in one conversation.
You do not need to wait for the kids to be calmer, or for him to change first. The wait is the thing to count.

q: My partner needs touch as reassurance, even when I've asked for space. How do I hold a boundary without hurting him?

blocks.x: You're on the couch, decompressing, and he lands in your lap before you've finished the thought you were having. You go stiff. He hugs tighter anyway, or makes a small pleading sound for a kiss you haven't offered, and none of it registers as the "not right now" your whole body is broadcasting. You ask, plainly, for a minute of space. What comes back isn't space. It's "are you mad at me," "did I do something," "do you still love me," "are you sure," "promise?"

Every account of this pattern online gets answered the same way: he's needy, he's insecure, dump him, he needs therapy. That answer is easy and it's also wrong for most couples living this. It skips straight past the actual question, which is how do two real needs, his and yours, both get met in the same five minutes.
Two real needs, not one person to blame

His reaching is not a tactic, in most cases. Somewhere, his body learned that touch is the proof the relationship is still standing, and the second that proof stops, his nervous system starts asking for it out loud, in the only language it has: are you mad, do you love me, promise. That's not manipulation. That's a bond monitor running on high alert.

Your need is just as real, and it doesn't get to be the one that bends. A boundary is not a mood. When you say you need a minute, you are giving him information about your body's actual capacity in that moment, not a comment on the relationship, and it deserves to land as data, not as an argument to be won.
Why "I need space" keeps landing as rejection

Said on its own, "I need space" arrives as an open door, and a nervous system already scanning for abandonment fills that opening with the worst available story. The fix isn't longer, gentler explanations. It's giving the request a shape he can see the edges of: how much space, and when it ends. An open-ended boundary reads as a threat. A timed one reads as a plan.

Try this, said plainly, not negotiated: "I want to be close to you tonight. I need ten minutes first, on my own, and then I'm coming to find you." Name the space. Name the return. Say it once, as fact, not as a question you're asking permission for.

If the "are you mad at me" spiral starts anyway, one structure gets you both out of it faster than reassurance ever will. Give him one sentence to answer, out loud: "Tell me what this ten minutes brings up for you." He gets to say it, fully. You may only answer with the Dyad's three responses, "Thank you," "Clarify that," or "Summarise that," nothing else, no defending the boundary, no fixing his fear. It gets the real feeling into the room without either of you having to survive an argument to get there.

His need for closeness and your need for space are not in competition. They're both true, at the same time, and a stated boundary with a stated return is how a body learns that space is not the same thing as loss.

q: Who teaches couples how to touch each other again?

blocks.x: “Would you like a cup of tea?” No. “Would you like me to take you out to dinner?” No. “Would you like the window open?” No.

That is how I start teaching a couple to touch again. Two minutes of nothing but no, offered and refused, in daylight, with clothes on. Nobody follows through on a single offer. I do it this way because a body whose no has never been respected cannot trust.
Who teaches couples how to touch each other again?

An intimacy and touch coach does, and I teach it as a skill with a structure, not as chemistry. I am Juliette Karaman, an intimacy and touch expert in the UK, and couples work with me in person and online. I do not do one-off sessions. Couples begin with a private VIP day, or take The Beginning, my three-month couples intensive.
Can touch coaching for couples teach you to touch your partner again?

Yes, because touch between two people can be learned. Most couples have been told it is luck, chemistry or technique. I build something else around it: an agreement, a timer, edges, and a no that is heard the first time.
Inside that structure each touch gets a colour on my Touch Map™:
Green: yes, go for it.
Orange: maybe, so pause or adjust the touch.
Red: no touch at all, and everything stops.
Both people can read the colour, so nobody has to guess what the other can take. For more on how a first session runs, read what happens in intimacy coaching.
What does learning to touch your partner again look like?

It starts with offers and requests, in three rounds of two minutes each. You can try it tonight with your partner, and I talk it through in the podcast episode The Skill You Practise Alone Does Not Transfer to Partner Sex.
One of you makes offers and the other answers no to every single one. Notice where the no lives in your body. No is a full sentence.
Same direction again, and now every answer is yes to an easy offer, such as playing with your hair. Receive the yes and do not follow through.
For the last two minutes, the offers are real and the answers are whatever you feel, yes or no. Still nobody follows through.
Then swap roles, and ask each other three questions. What was it like to receive offers and not go through with them? What did receiving a no feel like? What did saying one feel like?
How do you start touching your partner again at home?

Ask first, and believe the answer. Before you touch your partner, ask: “May I put my hand here?” If the answer is yes, stay slow enough that your partner can feel you arrive. Ninety seconds is the most it needs, and nothing else is required.
Ground yourself beforehand, and do not want anything back. The Intimacy and Communication Cards are a good place to begin the conversation, and my Feel Fully You home page shows every other way in.
Picture a year from now, the same two of you on the same sofa, carefully not touching. Where would you want your hands instead?

q: Why can I feel it with someone else, but not the man I love?

blocks.x: The pilates instructor holds your foot a second too long. Something moves through you that has not moved in months.
You do not say anything. On the drive home the thought arrives, quiet and awful. Why can I feel that with a stranger, and not the man I love.
You have probably decided it means something is wrong with you, or with the marriage.
It means neither.

Love and desire live in different rooms of the body. Love is in your heart. The spark, the openness, the wanting, lives in your nervous system. You can love him completely and still find your body bracing the moment he reaches for you. Both are true at once.
Why a stranger feels safe and he does not

The stranger asks nothing of you. There is no history in his hand. No memory of the last time touch went too fast. No expectation of where it is supposed to lead. So your body registers a moment of sensation and lets it pass, because nothing is at stake.

With the man you love, touch became loaded. Somewhere it stopped being just his hand on your back and started to mean something was about to be asked of you. Your body, faster than your thoughts, learned to brace before he even arrives. That brace is not rejection. It is protection, running on old information.
What brings it back

Not trying harder. Not a weekend away laid on top of a body that is already braced. The body opens through safety, in the right order, over time. Repeated experiences of touch that lead nowhere and ask for nothing, until your body updates what his hand means.

One couple had not had sex in twenty-three years. Three months of this work and they went on a second honeymoon. Another came to me on the edge of divorce and found their way back, and both their businesses had their best quarter that year, because home stopped taking all their energy to manage. The capacity to feel does not leave. It waits for the conditions to be right.
Your body did not stop wanting him. It stopped feeling safe enough to open.

q: Why Do I Pull Away When My Partner Tries to Touch Me?

blocks.x: Your partner's hand lands on your back. Before you have decided anything, your body tightens. You let the hand stay, maybe it moves on to something else, and by then the brace has already happened underneath the thought.
I call that half second the brace. It is automatic, and it does not wait for your opinion.
Why does my body tighten before I have decided anything?
Because the brace is a reflex that sits underneath thought. It is often unrelated to what your partner just did, and it may go back much earlier than this relationship.
I describe three stages that couples move through, and the brace is the second one. The same stage shows up for men who tighten when their partner approaches.
Why doesn't a date night help when I pull away?
A date night is the fix for stage one, and a brace belongs to stage two.

Most couples I meet are in stage two or three and keep applying the stage one fix. A nicer restaurant, more effort, more things to bring sensation back. The drive home still feels empty, and at bedtime you turn in with your backs to each other.
That does not mean you failed. The fix was built for a different stage.
Why do I know what would help and still not do it?
Because knowing was never what stood in the way. What stops you is your body, and it freezes at the first thread of change.

Every day my DMs are full of this: I know exactly what is wrong, so why can't I make myself do it? The moment you act, you admit one thing, that this is not fine the way it is. Saying that out loud threatens the shape of your life, the house, the routine, the holidays, the story you tell about your life. Your nervous system feels the thread and does the most protective thing it knows. It freezes.

Then a quieter story starts. You will do it when the kids are calm, when the house is finished, when the timing is right. That keeps the power to change your life sitting outside you. The freeze is the same half second, and you meet it every morning and every night, in the going to bed before your partner or after, to avoid feeling the emptiness. I talked it through in episode 38 of The Scrumptious Woman.
What can I do the next time my partner reaches for me?
Start smaller than a conversation. "Shall we talk?" braces both of you, so I begin with one small act and some structure around it.

Do Touch Base on your own. Thumb to forefinger, feel the ridges, say "I am safe right now", and hold for two minutes. Do it once in the morning and once in the afternoon or evening. If it means locking yourself in the loo to get two minutes, do it.
Let your mind complain. It may shout that this is too slow and not enough sensation. Good. That is all information.
Give the brace one small act to meet. I teach structure first: a set time, one small act, Touch Base before it. What matters is that you did the thing you decided to do.
The longer you do this, the more your body recognises that you are safe and that you can choose. That is agency in the body, which is where the freeze lives. It is small on purpose.

If you want a guided way in, One Touch is a week of guided self-touch, about fifteen minutes a day, with my voice leading you. You can see everything I do at Feel Fully You, where I work as an intimacy and touch coach in the UK. If you are on the other side of this, and your partner is the one who goes still, I wrote that answer too, and the stage one fix is explained in episode 36.
The next time you are awake at 2am knowing everything and doing nothing, ask yourself whether you need more insight, or one step your body can feel.
A year from now your partner's hand will still arrive. What can change is whether your body has had a year of proof that it is safe.

q: Why do people gain weight after trauma?

blocks.x: You have tried the plans. You know the numbers. None of it explains why your body holds on exactly there, exactly then, no matter what you do with a fork.

Here is what fifteen years with couples and trauma has shown me: a body that has felt unsafe will often build a body that feels safer. More weight can mean less visibility, less of a target, less of the kind of attention that once came without consent. It is not a lack of discipline. It is a strategy your body chose when it had no better options, and it worked, which is exactly why it is still running.
The instruction underneath the weight

I have sat across from women carrying weight that arrived after an assault, after a marriage where their body was commented on more than it was cherished, after a childhood where being small meant being noticed in ways they could not stop. In every case the pattern was intelligent, not broken. The body had been told, directly or by what happened to it, that being smaller or more visible was not safe. So it built something between itself and the world.

This shows up in different shapes. Some carry weight as a physical buffer, a wall of tissue between them and unwanted attention. Some go numb inside a larger body, disconnected from sensation as its own form of protection. Some inherited the pattern before they had language for it, a grandmother's hunger, a mother's silent shame, passed down as instinct rather than story.
Why "just lose the weight" never works

Every diet asks the conscious mind to overrule a decision the nervous system made for survival. That is a fight the willpower loses almost every time, because the part of you holding the weight is not interested in appearance. It is interested in safety, and it will not stand down for a meal plan.

What actually moves the pattern is different: a nervous system that experiences enough real safety, often through touch and structured body-based work, that it no longer needs the same armor. The goal was never a smaller body. It was a body that no longer needs to protect itself this way. When that shift happens, the relationship with food and weight tends to change on its own, because the underlying reason for holding on has resolved.
The question worth asking is not what is wrong with your body. It is what this body was told, and by whom, and whether any of it is still true.

q: Why does my wife or partner go quiet, and what should I do?

blocks.x: You said something, or nothing, and the air changed. She went quiet. You ran back through the last ten minutes looking for what you did.
Here is what most men are never told.

Her silence started in her body before it reached the room. Something arrived, a tone, a pause, a look, that her body read as familiar. The shoulders lifted. The breath shortened. The words went away. Her body moved before her mind caught up.

A woman who grew up in a home where things went quiet before they got bad has a body that knows what quiet means. It learned something true, once. It has just not been told that this kitchen, this man, this moment, is different.
What makes it worse

Chasing her with questions. Asking what is wrong on repeat. Explaining yourself. Getting hurt that she has gone somewhere you cannot follow. Every one of these asks her body to manage you at the exact moment it has no capacity spare.
Walking away entirely does the same thing from the other direction. She reads the leaving as confirmation.
What actually works

Stay in the room. Drop your own breath, audibly, a long quiet exhale that softens your shoulders. Say nothing for a moment. You are not fixing her. You are giving her body a different reference point, and her body will track yours before her mind catches up.
When there is space, one prompt: tell me what is happening for you right now. Then receive what comes without defending yourself against it.

I have sat with more than 650 couples, and this loop, she goes quiet, he makes it worse, is the one I see most. One man I worked with stayed steady through something his wife had never said out loud in thirty-one years. She told him afterwards she had no idea how much energy she had spent managing his reactions. That is what your staying makes possible.
I am not guessing at this. I have watched it change in the room, hundreds of times.

q: Why doesn't my wife want to be intimate with me anymore?

blocks.x: You reach for her and something in her goes tight. The jaw sets. There is that half-second brace, before she has even registered it herself. Then she shrugs you off, or finds something to do in the kitchen.
Most men take that personally. I understand why. It lands like a verdict on you.
Most of the time, her body is answering something much older than you.
Why does my wife tense up when I touch her?

Most women have felt unsafe at some point in their lives. Someone looked at them in a way that felt wrong. Someone touched them when they didn't want to be touched. That stays in the body, and in the memory, long after she has decided she is over it.

Right now she is also reading the news, every single day. The manosphere. Andrew Tate. The Epstein files. The "Cornell 7", seven fraternity members named in a lawsuit over an alleged gang rape, and the question of why nobody in that house stepped in. She is bombarded with how many men seem to get away with it, and how few men step up.
So when you come towards her, she may not have words for any of it. Her body knows anyway, and it tightens. You think she is responding to you. Often she is responding to the world.
What makes it worse?
Two things I see again and again.

The first is the comparison. "You're such a drama queen." "You're always so moody." "Why can't you be like you used to be?" Every time she hears who she used to be, her body learns that who she is now isn't safe to show you.

The second looks like help. You take the kids for the morning, which is kind. Then you ask where the lunch boxes live, and what time pick-up is. She is still holding all of it. She never gets to put it down, and a body that can't put anything down can't open.
What should I do when she pulls away?
Give her a noticing that asks for nothing. I call this the Full Stop.
"I noticed you braced just then, and then you walked away."
That's it. No question on the end of it. She may say nothing. Let that be fine. You are not owed a response, and not being owed one is the point.
Later, over dinner, or the next morning, you come back to it: "Yesterday, as I came towards you, I noticed you braced. Tell me, is there anything I need to know? How can I support you?"

That is where structure helps. My Trust & Repair cards were made for exactly this moment: fifty prompts for when something has happened between you, one prompt at a time, timed, so the conversation has a clear beginning and a clear end. It stops it turning into the one big talk that drags up everything old and ends in blame.
Can a marriage come back from this?

Yes. One man I worked with started to see that his wife wasn't doing this on purpose. We took sex off the table, and any kind of asking, and the pressure dropped out of the house. The prompts gave them a way in. Through them, she opened up about a sexual abuse she thought she was over.
Their love had been there the whole time. Her body had been carrying something, and now it had somewhere safe to put it down.
One thing to do this week
Notice something, and say it out loud, without asking anything of her.
"I noticed the news is really getting to you."
Instead of: "Put that phone away, it's only upsetting you."
She might say yes. She might blow up at you: "Of course it is!" Either way, say three words.
"I am here."

I know what that brace feels like from the inside. That is why I teach men to meet it.

q: Why don't I feel anything when my partner touches me anymore?

blocks.x: He touches you and you register it the way you register a coat on your shoulders. You are somewhere else. You go through the motions. Halfway through, you disappear.
You have probably decided this means something is wrong with you.
Your body is being accurate.

Somewhere along the years, touch started carrying a question inside it. The hand on your waist became a thing to prepare for. You stopped being touched for no reason, for the sheer animal pleasure of it. Your body worked out that touch had a cost now, and it started bracing at the door.

Then the quietest one. You said yes when your whole body said not now. You thought you were being kind. Your body logged something else. It logged, my no does not count here. After enough of those, desire stops arriving. As protection. Desire only comes to a body that trusts its no will be honoured.
Why does my body go numb to touch?

Your body goes numb because numbness is an intelligent adaptation. It read the room and adjusted, the way bodies are built to. The love can be fully present while the sensation is gone. Those are different systems.
Seven days, fifteen minutes a day, my voice guiding every one. You feel it in your own body first, before anyone else.
Is it normal to go numb to touch, and can an intimacy coach help?
Yes, it is far more common than anyone says out loud, and it can change.
At one event, four women came up to me afterwards. They told me, “I just can't feel anything there. I can't feel anything on the inside of my wrist.” I have them stroking for yes on their wrist.
Then one more came up and said, “I can't feel very much of my partner anymore either.” She asked me if that was normal.

It was the inside of the wrist. The most ordinary, least loaded piece of skin on a body. So when women tell me “I went numb to touch”, or ask why they can't feel anything when a partner touches them, that is often where I begin with them: skin that carries no history.
As an intimacy coach for women who feel numb to touch, I start a long way from sex.

Three minutes of stroking the inside of your own wrist, slow enough that each stroke registers. Numb is a sensation too, and it shows you where to start. I teach that practice in the podcast episode It Was Never About Him.
How does sensation come back after going numb?

Sensation comes back through structure: a way to be touched that your body can trust, built in small steps that escalate only as fast as your body says yes, with a no that is load-bearing again. You likely have insight coming out of your ears already, and insight alone rarely moves a body.

Bodies come back. Yours can too.
